| Full HD desktop | 1920 × 1080 | 2xl | xxl |

#### Tailwind and Bootstrap breakpoints

A breakpoint applies from its minimum width upwards. Below the first one, Tailwind applies the unprefixed (base) styles and Bootstrap its `xs` tier.

| Breakpoint | Tailwind CSS | Bootstrap 5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sm | 640 px | 576 px |
| md | 768 px | 768 px |
| lg | 1024 px | 992 px |
| xl | 1280 px | 1200 px |
| 2xl / xxl | 1536 px | 1400 px |

#### Why some sites stay blank

A site can tell browsers not to display it inside another page, using the `X-Frame-Options` header or a `frame-ancestors` rule in its Content Security Policy. Google, Facebook, banks and many others do this to prevent clickjacking, and no in-browser tester can get around it.

Your own site usually has no such rule, so it works. If yours does, test a staging copy without the header, or run the site locally and enter its `localhost` address.

#### What this test shows — and what it does not

- **It shows** how the layout responds to width and height: media queries, flexbox and grid changes, hidden menus, overflowing text and images.
- **It does not emulate** touch input, the device’s pixel density, or a mobile browser’s user agent — the page is still drawn by the browser you are using.
- For the last word on a real phone — Safari’s toolbar, the notch, keyboard behaviour — check on the device itself.
- An http address cannot be shown inside this https page, except `localhost`. Use the https address.

### FAQ

**Where does Responsive Design Tester run?**
Responsive Design Tester has to reach the network for a public lookup. The page says what leaves your device. Toolspire does not keep a copy of the query.

**How do I test if my website is responsive?**
Enter its address, press **Test**, and look at it on a phone, a tablet and a laptop side by side. Check that nothing overflows sideways, text stays readable and menus remain usable at every width.

**Can I test a site running on localhost?**
Yes. Type `localhost:3000` (or whichever port your dev server uses). Browsers allow a local page inside a secure page, so it works without any setup.

**Why is the frame blank or says “refused to connect”?**
The site forbids being shown inside other pages with `X-Frame-Options` or a Content Security Policy. Many large sites do. Test your own site, a staging copy or a local build instead.

**What screen sizes should I test?**
At least a small phone (360–390 px), a tablet (768 px), a laptop (1366 px) and a large desktop (1920 px). Then drag in any width where your design has a breakpoint.

**Is this the same as a real phone?**
For layout, yes — the frame is a true viewport of that size. It does not reproduce touch, pixel density or a different browser engine, so finish with a check on a real device.

**What are the Tailwind breakpoints?**
`sm` 640 px, `md` 768 px, `lg` 1024 px, `xl` 1280 px and `2xl` 1536 px. Each applies from that width upwards.

**Is the address I enter sent to you?**
No. Your browser loads the page directly from its own site, as if you had opened it in a tab. The address is remembered only in this tab so it is there next time.

## SSH Key Generator

URL: https://justtools.info/security-tools/ssh-key-generator/
Category: Security Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-13

Generate SSH keys on your device: Ed25519, RSA 4096 or ECDSA, with a passphrase, in OpenSSH, PEM or PuTTY.ppk format. Nothing is sent to a server.

### At a glance

- SSH Key Generator on Toolspire: generates **SSH key pairs in the browser**: **Ed25519** (recommended), **RSA** 2048, 3072 or 4096, and **ECDSA** P-256, P-384 or P-521.
- Writes the private key as **OpenSSH**, **PuTTY .ppk** (version 3), **PEM PKCS#8** or traditional PEM, and the public key as one line for `authorized_keys`.
- Protects the private key with an optional **passphrase** — bcrypt and AES-256 for OpenSSH, Argon2id for PuTTY, PBKDF2 for PKCS#8.
- Shows the **SHA-256 and MD5 fingerprints** and the same **randomart** picture that `ssh-keygen -lv` prints.
- Keys are checked against the real tools: `ssh-keygen` reads the generated files, derives the same public key and prints the same fingerprint.
- An Ed25519 public key is only **68 characters** of Base64; an RSA 4096 one is 716.
- Made with your browser’s own cryptography (Web Crypto). **The private key is not sent to us, stored or logged**, and is gone when you close the tab.

### Features

- **Every common key type**: Ed25519 for new keys, RSA for old servers, ECDSA where NIST curves are required.
- **OpenSSH, PEM or PuTTY**: Download the format your tool wants — no separate conversion step.
- **Passphrase protection**: Encrypt the private key before it ever touches your disk.
- **Fingerprint and randomart**: Verify the key against what your server or Git host shows.
- **Change without regenerating**: Edit the comment, passphrase or format and keep the same key.
- **Nothing leaves the page**: No server takes part. The private key is hidden on screen until you choose to show it.

### How to generate an SSH key

1. **Choose the key type** — Keep **Ed25519** unless a server or device needs RSA or ECDSA.
2. **Add a comment and passphrase** — The comment labels the key (your email works well). A passphrase encrypts the private key so a stolen file is useless.
3. **Generate** — Press **Generate key pair**. Ed25519 is instant; RSA 4096 takes a few seconds.
4. **Save both files** — Download the private key into your `.ssh` folder and keep it secret. Copy the public key to the server, GitHub or GitLab.

### Guide

#### Which SSH key type should I use?

| Type | Public key length | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ed25519 | 68 characters | Always, unless something refuses it. Fast, small and secure. |
| RSA 4096 | 716 characters | An old server, appliance or cloud service accepts only RSA. |
| RSA 2048 | 372 characters | A system limits the key size. The smallest RSA still accepted. |
| ECDSA P-256 | 140 characters | A policy or hardware token requires NIST curves. |

#### Where the files go

- The **private key** (`id_ed25519`) lives in the `.ssh` folder of your home directory and must be readable only by you: `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.
- The **public key** (`id_ed25519.pub`) is added as one line to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` on each server you log in to. `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub user@server` does this for you.
- For **GitHub** or **GitLab**, paste the public key under Settings → SSH keys, then test with `ssh -T git@github.com`.
- For **PuTTY** and **WinSCP**, choose the `.ppk` format and load the file under Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials.

#### The same key with ssh-keygen

On a computer with OpenSSH installed, the command line does the same job: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"` for Ed25519, or `ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096` for RSA. The files from this page are in the same formats, and `ssh-keygen -y -f id_ed25519` will print the public key back from the private one.

#### Is it safe to generate a key in the browser?

This page has no server side. The key is made by your browser’s cryptography from its secure random-number generator, and it is never sent, saved or logged — you can open the browser’s network panel and see that nothing is transmitted when you press Generate.

That said, the safest key is one that never leaves the machine that uses it. For keys that guard production systems, generate them on that machine with `ssh-keygen`, and always set a passphrase. Use this page when you cannot install tools, need a `.ppk` quickly, or want a key for testing.

### FAQ

**Where does SSH Key Generator run?**
SSH Key Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Should I choose Ed25519 or RSA?**
**Ed25519.** It is shorter, faster and at least as secure as RSA 4096, and every current SSH server, GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket accept it. Choose RSA only for older systems that do not.

**Do I need a passphrase?**
It is strongly recommended. Without one, anyone who copies the private key file can log in as you. With one, the file is encrypted and useless without the passphrase. An SSH agent means you type it only once per session.

**How do I add the key to GitHub?**
Copy the **public key**, open GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, paste it and save. Then run `ssh -T git@github.com` to check the connection.

**How do I use the key with PuTTY?**
Choose **PuTTY (.ppk)** as the private key format, download the file, and select it in PuTTY under Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials. To convert an existing key instead, use the [PEM to PPK converter](https://justtools.info/security-tools/pem-to-ppk/).

**What is the fingerprint for?**
It is a short hash of the public key. Servers and Git hosts show it so you can confirm, at a glance, that they hold the key you think they do. The randomart is the same fingerprint drawn as a picture.

**I lost the passphrase. Can it be recovered?**
No. The private key is encrypted with it and there is no back door. Generate a new key pair and replace the old public key on your servers.

**Can I change the comment or passphrase later?**
Yes. On this page, edit them and press **Update the files** to keep the same key. For a key you already saved, `ssh-keygen -p -f id_ed25519` changes the passphrase and `-c` the comment.

**Is my private key sent to your server?**
No. There is no server involved: generation happens in this tab, and the key exists only in this tab until you download it.

## JSON to TypeScript

URL: https://justtools.info/developer-tools/json-to-typescript/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-13

Generate TypeScript interfaces, types or Zod schemas from JSON online. Finds optional properties, unions and nested types. Free, private, without uploading.

### At a glance

- JSON to TypeScript on Toolspire: turns JSON into **TypeScript interfaces**, **type aliases** or **Zod schemas** with inferred types, straight away as you type.
- Every object in a list is combined into one type: a property missing from some objects becomes **optional** (`coupon?: string`), and a value seen with several types becomes a **union** (`string | number`).
- Nested objects get their own named types taken from their keys — `address` → `Address`, `orders` → `Order[]` — or are written inline. Places with the same name and structure share one type.
- Objects whose keys are IDs or dates, such as `{"1042": {…}, "1043": {…}}`, are typed as `Record<string, …>` instead of one property per ID.
- What the sample cannot show is reported instead of guessed: a value that is always `null` is typed `null`, and an empty list `unknown[]`, each listed with its path.
- Zod output declares every schema before it is used and adds a `z.infer` type for each one.
- Accepts JSON with comments, trailing commas and single quotes, and points to the exact line and column of real errors.
- Runs in this tab: the API responses you paste are not sent to us.

### Features

- **Three output styles**: `interface`, `type` or a Zod schema with its inferred type. Switch between them without pasting again.
- **Optional properties found for you**: Paste a list of records and every property that is missing from some of them is marked with `?`, with the paths listed below the result.
- **Readable type names**: Types are named from their keys and list items in the singular: `categories` gives `Category[]`. Name clashes are resolved, and names that would hide built-ins like `Date` are avoided.
- **Honest about gaps**: A `null` or an empty list tells nothing about the real type. Those places are listed so you can fill them in, rather than hidden behind `any`.
- **Your conventions**: Choose the root name, `export`, `readonly`, all-optional properties, inline or named nested types, and 2 spaces, 4 spaces or tabs.
- **Private**: Responses with tokens, customer data or internal fields stay on your device. Nothing is sent to a server.

### How to convert JSON to TypeScript

1. **Add your JSON** — Paste a JSON object or array — an API response, a config, a database record — or click **Open file**.
2. **Pick the output** — Choose **Interface**, **Type** or **Zod schema**, and set the root type name under **Options**.
3. **Read the notes** — Below the result, check which properties were made optional and which values had no type to infer.
4. **Copy or download** — Copy the code into your project or download it as a .ts file.

### Guide

#### How JSON values become types

| JSON | TypeScript | Zod |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"name": "Asha"` | `name: string` | `z.string()` |
| `"id": 1042` | `id: number` | `z.number()` |
| `"active": true` | `active: boolean` | `z.boolean()` |
| `"roles": ["admin"]` | `roles: string[]` | `z.array(z.string())` |
| `"address": {…}` | `address: Address` | `addressSchema` |
| in some objects only | `coupon?: string` | `z.string().optional()` |
| text in one object, `null` in another | `note: string | null` | `z.string().nullable()` |
| a number in one object, text in another | `value: string | number` | `z.union([z.string(), z.number()])` |
| `"avatar": null` every time | `avatar: null` | `z.null()` |
| `"tags": []` | `tags: unknown[]` | `z.array(z.unknown())` |
| `"extra": {}` | `extra: Record<string, unknown>` | `z.record(z.string(), z.unknown())` |

#### Getting better types

- Paste a **list of several records** rather than one. Optional properties and unions can only be found by comparing objects.
- Include a record where nullable fields have a value, so `avatar: null` becomes `avatar: string | null`.
- Types come from the sample, not from the API’s rules. A property present in every sample is typed as required even if the API may omit it — use **Make every property optional** for partial data.
- Dates, emails and URLs are strings in JSON, so they are typed `string`. Add stricter checks in your Zod schema where you need them.
- Property names that are not valid identifiers, such as `last-login`, are written in quotes: `'last-login': string`.

#### Interface, type or Zod?

An **interface** and a **type** describe the same object shape; use whichever your codebase prefers. Both exist only while compiling and add nothing to the code that runs.

A **Zod schema** also checks data at run time. Parse an API response with it and you get an error when the response does not match, plus the TypeScript type from `z.infer` — so the type and the check never drift apart. The generated code needs the `zod` package in your project.

### FAQ

**Where does JSON to TypeScript run?**
JSON to TypeScript runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Is my JSON uploaded anywhere?**
No. The types are generated in this tab, so API responses and internal data stay on this device.

**How does it decide a property is optional?**
When a list contains several objects, they are combined into one type. A property that some of them do not have is marked optional with `?`. With a single object there is nothing to compare, so every property is required.

**Why is a property typed null or unknown[]?**
The sample held only `null`, or only an empty list, at that place, so the real type cannot be known. The tool lists these paths below the result. Paste a sample with real values there, or edit the type by hand. Turn on **Use any where the type is unknown** if you prefer `any`.

**Can it generate a Zod schema?**
Yes. Choose **Zod schema** to get `z.object(…)` schemas with `.optional()`, `.nullable()`, unions, arrays and records, each followed by its `z.infer` type. Nested schemas are declared before the ones that use them, and the code runs on both Zod 3 and Zod 4.

**How are the types named?**
From the property key, in PascalCase: `shipping_address` becomes `ShippingAddress`. Items of a list use the singular (`orders` → `Order`). If two different structures would get the same name, the parent’s name is added, as in `OfficeAddress`.

**What about an object with IDs as keys?**
An object whose keys are all numbers, UUIDs, long hex IDs or dates is treated as a lookup table and typed as `Record<string, …>`, with the values combined into one type.

**Can I paste JSON with comments or trailing commas?**
Yes. Comments, trailing commas, single quotes and unquoted keys are repaired and listed. Real mistakes are reported with their line and column.

## JSON to YAML Converter

URL: https://justtools.info/developer-tools/json-to-yaml/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-13

JSON to YAML Converter on Toolspire. Convert JSON to YAML and YAML to JSON online. Quotes yes, no and 0755 so every parser reads them the same.

### At a glance

- JSON to YAML Converter on Toolspire: converts **JSON to YAML** and **YAML to JSON**, straight away as you type. Switching direction carries the result across.
- **Safe quoting**: text such as `yes`, `no`, `on`, `0755`, `1:30` and `2026-01-15` is written in quotes, because YAML 1.1 tools like PyYAML and Ansible would otherwise read it as true or false, a number or a date.
- Numbers are copied digit for digit: `1.50` stays `1.50`, and a 20-digit ID is not rounded.
- When reading YAML you choose **YAML 1.2** (the current standard) or **YAML 1.1**. Every unquoted value whose meaning depends on that choice is listed with its line number.
- Anchors, aliases and merge keys (`<<`) are replaced by the data they point to, and several documents separated by `---` become one JSON array.
- Mistakes are reported with their **line and column**. A key written twice in one mapping is refused rather than silently overwritten.
- Layout options: 2 or 4 spaces, quotes only where needed or on every string, lists indented or level with their key, short lists on one line, sorted keys and wrapping at 80 or 120 columns.
- Runs in this tab: the configs and API responses you paste are not sent to us.

### Features

- **Both directions**: JSON → YAML and YAML → JSON in one tool. Convert a file, edit it, and switch direction to turn it back.
- **No Norway problem**: The country code `NO`, the answer `yes` and the mode `0755` keep their quotes, so no parser turns them into false, true or 493.
- **Shows what is ambiguous**: Paste YAML with a bare `no` or `0755` and you are told how YAML 1.1 and 1.2 each read it, and on which line.
- **Exact numbers**: Prices, version numbers and long IDs are written exactly as they were, not passed through a floating-point number.
- **Exact error locations**: Bad indentation, a missing quote or a duplicate key is reported with its line and column, and one click jumps to it.
- **Private**: Kubernetes manifests, Compose files and CI configs are converted on your device. Nothing is sent to a server.

### How to convert JSON to YAML

1. **Add your JSON** — Paste JSON into the input, or click **Open file** to load a .json file. Comments and trailing commas are accepted.
2. **Choose the layout** — Pick 2 or 4 spaces, and open **Options** for quote style, list indentation, sorted keys or short lists on one line.
3. **Check the result** — The YAML appears as you type. If the JSON has a mistake, its line and column are shown.
4. **Copy or download** — Copy the YAML or download it as a .yaml file. Choose **YAML → JSON** to convert in the other direction.

### Guide

#### How JSON maps to YAML

| JSON | YAML |
| --- | --- |
| `{"name": "shop", "port": 8080}` | `name: shop` and `port: 8080` on separate lines |
| `"tags": ["api", "v2"]` | `tags:` followed by `- api` and `- v2` |
| `"db": {"host": "x"}` | `db:` followed by an indented `host: x` |
| `"debug": "no"` | `debug: "no"` (quoted, so it stays text) |
| `"price": 1.50` | `price: 1.50` (digits kept) |
| `"note": "line one\nline two"` | a `|-` block with one line of text per line |
| `"owner": null`, `"tags": []`, `"extra": {}` | `owner: null`, `tags: []`, `extra: {}` |

#### The same YAML, read two ways

YAML 1.2 has been the standard since 2009, but many widely used tools still follow YAML 1.1, and the two disagree about unquoted values. This is why a list of country codes can end up containing `false` instead of `NO` — the “Norway problem”.

| Written in YAML | YAML 1.2 reads | YAML 1.1 reads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `debug: no` | the text “no” | false |
| `country: NO` | the text “NO” | false |
| `mode: 0755` | the number 755 | the number 493 (octal) |
| `time: 1:30` | the text “1:30” | the number 90 (base 60) |
| `port: 0o17` | the number 15 | the text “0o17” |
| `on: push` | a key named “on” | a key named true |
| `date: 2026-01-15` | the text “2026-01-15” | a date |

#### What YAML features become in JSON

- Anchors (`&name`) and aliases (`*name`) are replaced by a full copy of the data, and merge keys (`<<: *name`) are merged into the mapping.
- Several documents separated by `---` become one array, with one entry per document.
- Block text written with `|` keeps its line breaks; text written with `>` is joined into one line.
- Comments are dropped, because JSON has nowhere to keep them.
- `.inf` and `.nan` become `null`, since JSON has no way to write them. Binary data (`!!binary`) stays as Base64 text.
- Keys that are not text, such as numbers or lists, are turned into text, because every JSON key is a string.

### FAQ

**Where does JSON to YAML Converter run?**
JSON to YAML Converter runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Is it safe to convert config files with secrets here?**
Yes. The conversion runs in this tab, so manifests, environment files and API responses are not sent to us or stored.

**Why are some strings in quotes and others not?**
YAML only needs quotes when text could be read as something else. With **Safe for YAML 1.1 tools** on, that includes `yes`, `no`, `on`, `off`, numbers with a leading zero, values like `1:30` and dates. Choose **Double** or **Single** under Quotes to quote every string instead.

**What is the difference between YAML 1.1 and YAML 1.2?**
They read unquoted values differently. In YAML 1.1, `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are booleans, `0755` is an octal number and `1:30` is 90. In YAML 1.2 the first group is plain text and `0755` is 755. PyYAML and Ansible follow 1.1; newer parsers follow 1.2. This tool tells you when your YAML contains such values.

**Why did my key “y” or “on” get quotes?**
YAML 1.1 treats `y`, `n`, `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` as booleans even when they are keys, so some parsers would turn the key `on` into `true`. The quotes prevent that. Turn off **Safe for YAML 1.1 tools** if you only use YAML 1.2 parsers.

**Are comments kept when converting YAML to JSON?**
No. JSON has no comments, so they are left out, and the tool says so below the result.

**Can I convert a file with several YAML documents?**
Yes. Documents separated by `---`, as in many Kubernetes files, become one JSON array with an entry for each document.

**Does it accept JSON with comments or trailing commas?**
Yes. Comments, trailing commas, single quotes and unquoted keys are repaired, and the tool lists what it fixed. Real mistakes are reported with their line and column.

**Is .yml different from .yaml?**
No. Both extensions hold the same format. The download uses .yaml, the extension the YAML project recommends; rename it to .yml if your tool expects that.

## YAML to XML Converter

URL: https://justtools.info/developer-tools/yaml-to-xml/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-13

YAML to XML Converter on Toolspire: Convert YAML to XML and XML to YAML online. Handles attributes, lists, anchors and the root element.

### At a glance

- YAML to XML Converter on Toolspire: converts **YAML to XML** and **XML to YAML**, straight away as you type. Switching direction carries the result across.
- Keys that start with **@** become XML attributes and **#text** becomes the text of an element — the same convention as the XML to JSON converter, so data converts there and back unchanged.
- A YAML list **repeats the element** (`<tag>a</tag><tag>b</tag>`) or **wraps each item** (`<tags><item>a</item>…</tags>`), whichever your XML needs.
- XML needs exactly one root: YAML with several top-level keys, a top-level list or several documents is wrapped in a root element you can name.
- Anchors, aliases and merge keys (`<<`) are written out in full, and numbers keep their digits: `799.00` stays `799.00`.
- From XML, text that YAML tools could misread — `00482`, `yes`, `2026-01-15` — is written in quotes, so leading zeros and codes survive.
- Mistakes in the YAML or the XML are reported with their **line and column**.
- Runs in this tab: nothing you paste is uploaded.

### Features

- **Both directions**: YAML → XML and XML → YAML in one tool, with options for each side. Convert, edit and convert back.
- **Attributes and text**: `"@id": 7` becomes `id="7"`, and `#text` holds the text of an element that also has attributes. Choose `_`, `-` or `$` as the prefix instead.
- **Always valid XML**: A root element is added when needed, keys that are not valid XML names are fixed and listed, and `&`, `<` and `>` are escaped or put in CDATA.
- **Clean, safe YAML**: Numbers and booleans are converted, while IDs with leading zeros and words like `no` stay quoted text that every YAML parser reads the same.
- **Exact error locations**: A wrong indent or an unclosed tag is reported with its line and column, and one click jumps to it in the input.
- **Private**: Build files, configs and feeds are converted on your device. Nothing is sent to a server.

### How to convert YAML to XML

1. **Add your YAML** — Paste YAML into the input, or click **Open file** to load a .yaml or .yml file.
2. **Mark attributes** — Give a key the prefix `@` (in quotes, as `"@id"`) to make it an attribute, and use `#text` for the text of that element.
3. **Adjust the options** — Open **Options** to name the root and item elements, wrap list items, use CDATA or drop the XML declaration.
4. **Copy or download** — Copy the XML or download it as a .xml file. Choose **XML → YAML** to convert in the other direction.

### Guide

#### How YAML becomes XML

| YAML | XML |
| --- | --- |
| `name: Asha` | `<name>Asha</name>` |
| `user:` with `"@id": 7` inside | `<user id="7">…</user>` |
| `price:` with `"@currency": INR` and `"#text": 799.00` | `<price currency="INR">799.00</price>` |
| `tag:` with `- a` and `- b` | `<tag>a</tag><tag>b</tag>`, or `<tag><item>a</item><item>b</item></tag>` with **Wrap items** |
| `notes: null` or `notes: ""` | `<notes/>` |
| `first name: x` | `<first_name>x</first_name>` (renamed, and reported) |
| two top-level keys | both wrapped in `<root>` |

#### How XML becomes YAML

| XML | YAML |
| --- | --- |
| `<name>Asha</name>` | `name: Asha` |
| `<user id="7"/>` | `user:` with `"@id": 7` inside |
| `<tag>a</tag><tag>b</tag>` | `tag:` with `- a` and `- b` |
| `<sku>00482</sku>` | `sku: "00482"` (leading zero kept) |
| `<answer>yes</answer>` | `answer: "yes"` (quoted, so it stays text) |
| `<count>42</count>`, `<live>true</live>` | `count: 42`, `live: true` |
| `<![CDATA[<b>bold</b>]]>` | `<b>bold</b>` as plain text |

#### Good to know

- YAML reserves the `@` character, so attribute keys must be written in quotes: `"@id": 7`. Choose the `_` prefix in **Options** for keys that need no quotes, such as `_id`.
- An empty YAML list has no XML form when elements repeat, so it is left out and reported. **Wrap items** keeps it as an empty element.
- YAML comments are not carried over, and XML comments and the `<?xml ?>` declaration are dropped when converting to YAML.
- Several YAML documents separated by `---` become one `<item>` each inside the root element.
- When reading YAML you can choose YAML 1.2 or 1.1. Under 1.1, `debug: no` becomes `<debug>false</debug>`; under 1.2 it stays `<debug>no</debug>`.

### FAQ

**Where does YAML to XML Converter run?**
YAML to XML Converter runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**How do I create XML attributes from YAML?**
Start the key with `@` and put it in quotes, because YAML reserves that character: `"@id": 7` inside `user:` gives `<user id="7">`. To add text to the same element, use the key `"#text"`.

**Why was my data wrapped in a root element?**
An XML document must have exactly one top-level element. If your YAML has one top-level key, that key becomes the root. With several keys, a list or several documents, a `<root>` element is added — rename it under **Options**.

**Is it safe to convert private configuration files?**
Yes. Everything runs in this tab. The YAML and XML you paste or open are not sent to us or stored.

**Why are some values quoted in the YAML?**
Values such as `00482`, `yes` or `2026-01-15` would be read by some YAML tools as a number, true or a date. Quoting keeps them as the text the XML contained. Turn off **Safe for YAML 1.1 tools** to quote less.

**What happens to anchors and aliases?**
XML has no equivalent, so every alias (`*name`) and merge key (`<<`) is replaced by a full copy of the data it refers to.

**Why is a single element not a list in the YAML?**
An element becomes a list only when it repeats. Turn on **Always use lists** so the structure is the same for one item or many.

**Does it work with pom.xml, RSS or SVG files?**
Yes — any well-formed XML. Use **Remove namespace prefixes** for shorter keys, or **Ignore attributes** when you only need the elements.

## .htaccess Generator

URL: https://justtools.info/developer-tools/htaccess-generator/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-14

.htaccess generator for Apache 2.4: 301 redirects, force HTTPS and www, security headers, password protection, compression and caching, each explained.

### At a glance

- .htaccess Generator on Toolspire: builds an **.htaccess file for Apache 2.4** from switches and short forms: HTTPS, www, redirects, error pages, security, passwords, compression, caching and URL rewriting.
- Every kind of rule was loaded into a real Apache 2.4 server and checked with requests while the tool was built.
- Rules that need an optional module are wrapped in `<IfModule>`, so a server without it skips them instead of showing “500 Internal Server Error”.
- Redirects can be **301, 302, 307, 308 or 410**, for one URL, a whole folder or a regular expression — or pasted as a list. Loops, missing targets and duplicates are flagged.
- The HTTPS and www rules are ordered so that `http://www.` reaches `https://` without www in **one redirect**, with an option for sites behind Cloudflare or a load balancer.
- Includes an **.htpasswd line maker**: the password is hashed with bcrypt in this tab, in the `$2y$` form Apache expects.
- Presets for a typical site, **WordPress**, a static site or single-page app, and a PHP app.
- Runs in this tab. Your domain, redirects and passwords are not uploaded; your choices are saved on your device only.

### Features

- **Explained, not just generated**: Each section of the file starts with a comment saying what it does, so you can read it again in a year. Switch the comments off for a compact file.
- **Catches mistakes first**: A redirect to itself, a relative .htpasswd path, an invalid IP address, HSTS without HTTPS — each is pointed out before the file reaches your server.
- **Safe by default**: Module checks keep a missing module from taking the site down, and hidden files such as .env and .git are closed while /.well-known/ stays open for certificates.
- **Redirects in bulk**: Paste old and new paths from a spreadsheet, one pair per line. A line with only an old path becomes “410 Gone”.
- **Password protection with the hash**: Get both halves: the rules for .htaccess and the bcrypt line for .htpasswd, for a whole folder or a single file.
- **Private**: Nothing is sent to a server: the file is written, and the password hashed, in this tab.

### How to create an .htaccess file

1. **Pick a starting point** — Choose **Recommended basics**, **WordPress**, **Static site or SPA** or **PHP app** — or start empty.
2. **Switch on what you need** — Open each group — HTTPS and www, redirects, security, speed — and turn rules on. Read any warning that appears above the file.
3. **Download the file** — Click **Download** (or **Copy**). The file is saved as htaccess.txt because computers hide files that start with a dot.
4. **Upload and rename** — Keep a copy of your current .htaccess, upload the new file to the top folder of the site (often public_html) and rename it to .htaccess.
5. **Test straight away** — Open the site, an old URL you redirected and a page that does not exist. If you see “500 Internal Server Error”, put the old file back.

### Guide

#### What each option writes

| Option | Rule | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Force HTTPS | `RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !=on` then `RewriteRule ^ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [L,R=301]` | http:// goes to https://, keeping the path and query |
| Remove www | `RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^www\.(.+)$ [NC]` | www.example.com goes to example.com |
| Moved page | `RedirectMatch 301 ^/old-page/?$ /new-page` | that URL only, with or without a final slash |
| Moved folder | `Redirect 301 /blog /news` | /blog/post goes to /news/post |
| Removed page | `RedirectMatch gone ^/old-page/?$` | “410 Gone”: the page was removed on purpose |
| Folder listings off | `Options -Indexes` | a folder without an index page shows 403 |
| Hide dot files | `RedirectMatch 404 "/\.(?!well-known(?:/|$))"` | .env and .git answer 404 |
| Custom 404 page | `ErrorDocument 404 /404.html` | your page, still with status 404 |
| Caching | `ExpiresByType text/css "access plus 1 month"` | returning visitors reuse the file |
| Compression | `AddOutputFilterByType DEFLATE text/html …` | text is sent with gzip, or Brotli where available |

#### Which redirect code to use

| Code | Meaning | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 301 | Moved permanently | a page or site has a new address for good — search engines move its ranking to the new URL |
| 302 | Found (temporary) | the page will come back, such as during maintenance or a short campaign |
| 307 | Temporary, method kept | as 302, when forms that POST must keep working |
| 308 | Permanent, method kept | as 301, for APIs and forms that POST |
| 410 | Gone | the page was removed on purpose and has no replacement |

#### Before you upload

- .htaccess works on **Apache** and LiteSpeed. Nginx ignores it — check with your host if you are unsure which server you have.
- The file belongs in the site’s top folder. Rules apply to that folder and everything under it.
- The rewrite rules assume the site is at the root of the domain, not in a subfolder such as example.com/shop/.
- One mistyped line anywhere in the file causes “500 Internal Server Error” on every page. Keep the old file so you can restore it in seconds.
- Behind Cloudflare’s “Flexible” SSL or a load balancer, switch on **Behind Cloudflare or a load balancer**. Without it, Force HTTPS redirects for ever.
- Browsers remember 301 redirects and HSTS for a long time. Test with 302 first if you are unsure, and leave HSTS off until HTTPS works on every page.
- For PHP that does not run as an Apache module (PHP-FPM, most shared hosts today), the PHP limits are skipped; put them in a .user.ini file instead.

### FAQ

**Where does .htaccess Generator run?**
.htaccess Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Where do I put the .htaccess file?**
In the top folder of your website — usually `public_html`, `htdocs` or `www`. The file must be named exactly `.htaccess`, with the dot and no extension. File managers often hide it; turn on “show hidden files”.

**Why is the download called htaccess.txt?**
Browsers and operating systems hide or rename files whose names start with a dot. Upload htaccess.txt and rename it to `.htaccess` on the server, or use **Copy** and paste into your host’s file editor.

**My site shows “500 Internal Server Error” after uploading. What now?**
Put your previous .htaccess back (or rename the new one) and the site returns at once. The usual causes are a module your host has disabled or a rule your host does not allow in .htaccess. Keep **Skip rules whose module is missing** on, then add the groups back one at a time to find the one your server rejects.

**How do I redirect HTTP to HTTPS and www to non-www together?**
Turn on **Force HTTPS** and choose **Remove www**. The rules are written in an order that sends `http://www.example.com/page` to `https://example.com/page` in a single redirect.

**Is the password I type for .htpasswd safe?**
Yes. It is hashed with bcrypt inside your browser and never leaves it; only the finished line is shown. It is not saved with your other choices either.

**Does this work with WordPress?**
Yes. Choose the **WordPress** preset: your rules are placed above the standard `# BEGIN WordPress` block, which WordPress keeps rewriting on its own. Anything above that block is left alone.

**Will it work on Nginx or IIS?**
No. .htaccess is read by Apache and LiteSpeed only. Nginx needs the same rules in its server configuration, and IIS uses web.config.

**Are my settings stored anywhere?**
Only in this tab’s local storage, so they are still there when you come back. Nothing is uploaded. Clearing the site data for Toolspire removes them.

## Chemical Equation Balancer

URL: https://justtools.info/education-tools/chemical-equation-balancer/
Category: Education Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-14

Chemical Equation Balancer on Toolspire. Balance any chemical equation online, redox and ionic included. See the atom count on each side, molar masses.

### At a glance

- Chemical Equation Balancer on Toolspire: balances chemical equations with the **smallest whole-number coefficients**, worked out exactly — never by trial and error or rounding.
- Handles brackets (`Ca3(PO4)2`), hydrates (`CuSO4.5H2O`), complex ions (`[Fe(CN)6]^4-`), states of matter and reversible arrows.
- Balances **ionic equations and half-reactions** by charge as well as atoms: `MnO4- + Fe2+ + H+ → Mn2+ + Fe3+ + H2O` becomes 1, 5, 8 → 1, 5, 4.
- Shows a check table — atoms of each element, total charge and mass on both sides — so you can see the equation is balanced.
- Gives the **molar mass** of every substance from IUPAC standard atomic weights, and works out the grams and moles of everything from one amount you enter.
- Finds the **limiting reactant** and how much of the others is left over when you enter amounts for two or more reactants.
- Names the reaction type where the pattern settles it: synthesis, decomposition, combustion, single or double displacement, neutralisation.
- When an equation cannot be balanced, it says why: an element on one side only, a substance on the wrong side, or charges that cannot match.

### Features

- **Exact, every time**: The coefficients come from solving the element and charge equations in fractions, so even long redox equations with coefficients in the hundreds are right.
- **Type it the way you write it**: H2SO4, Fe^3+, SO4^2-, e-, CuSO4.5H2O — or paste H₂SO₄ and Fe³⁺ straight from a document. Any arrow works: ->, =, → or ⇌.
- **Proof on the page**: Every element is counted on the left and the right, with the charge and the mass, so you can show your working.
- **Stoichiometry built in**: Enter grams or moles of one substance to get all the others; enter two reactants to find the limiting one and the excess.
- **Helpful when it fails**: A wrong capital letter, a missing product or an unbalanced charge gets a plain explanation instead of “error”.
- **Private and free**: Everything is calculated in this tab. No account, no limits.

### How to balance a chemical equation

1. **Type the equation** — Write the reactants, an arrow and the products, with + between substances: `C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O`. Leave the coefficients out.
2. **Use capitals and digits** — Element symbols need their capital letters (`Co` is cobalt, `CO` is carbon monoxide). Type subscripts as plain digits and charges after `^`: `Fe^3+`.
3. **Read the result** — The balanced equation appears as you type, with the reaction type and a table that counts each element on both sides.
4. **Work out amounts** — In the amounts table, type the grams or moles of one substance to see how much of each other substance reacts or forms.

### Guide

#### How to type formulas

| To write | Type | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A subscript | the digit after the symbol | `H2O`, `C6H12O6` |
| A group in brackets | ( ) or [ ] with a digit after | `Ca(OH)2`, `Al2(SO4)3`, `K4[Fe(CN)6]` |
| Water of crystallisation | a dot or * | `CuSO4.5H2O` |
| A charge | ^ then the charge | `Fe^3+`, `SO4^2-`, `NH4^+` |
| An electron | e- | `Fe^3+ + e- -> Fe^2+` |
| A state | (s), (l), (g) or (aq) after the formula | `NaCl(aq)` |
| The arrow | -> or = (⇌ or <-> for reversible) | `N2 + H2 <-> NH3` |

#### Worked examples

| You type | Balanced |
| --- | --- |
| `H2 + O2 -> H2O` | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O |
| `Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3` | 4 Fe + 3 O₂ → 2 Fe₂O₃ |
| `C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O` | C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O |
| `Al + H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + H2` | 2 Al + 3 H₂SO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3 H₂ |
| `KMnO4 + HCl -> KCl + MnCl2 + H2O + Cl2` | 2 KMnO₄ + 16 HCl → 2 KCl + 2 MnCl₂ + 8 H₂O + 5 Cl₂ |
| `Cr2O7^2- + H+ + e- -> Cr^3+ + H2O` | Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14 H⁺ + 6 e⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ + 7 H₂O |

#### How the balancing works

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of every element on both sides, and the same total charge. Each element gives one equation in the unknown coefficients: for hydrogen in H₂ + O₂ → H₂O, twice the coefficient of H₂ must equal twice the coefficient of H₂O.

The tool solves all of those equations together, exactly, and scales the answer to the smallest whole numbers. If there is no solution, the equation cannot be balanced as written — usually a formula is wrong or a substance is missing. If there is more than one independent solution, the equation is really two reactions written as one (for example C + O₂ → CO + CO₂), and the tool tells you so.

#### Digits before a + or − sign

Plain text cannot tell a charge from a subscript: `Fe3+` should be Fe³⁺ but `I3-` is I₃⁻. The tool reads a digit before the sign as the charge on a single atom (`Fe3+`, `Cu2+`, `O2-`) and as a subscript in anything larger (`MnO4-`, `NH4+`); two digits are split (`SO42-` is SO₄²⁻). If that reading cannot be balanced it tries the other, and it always shows how each ion was read. Write `Fe^3+` or `I3^-` to leave no doubt.

### FAQ

**Where does Chemical Equation Balancer run?**
Chemical Equation Balancer runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Why does it say an element appears on only one side?**
Atoms cannot appear or vanish in a reaction, so every element must be on both sides. Check for a missing product or reactant, and for typing slips such as `CL` for `Cl` or `NA` for `Na`.

**Can it balance redox equations?**
Yes. Molecular redox equations such as `KMnO4 + HCl -> KCl + MnCl2 + H2O + Cl2` are balanced directly. For ionic ones, include the H⁺ or OH⁻ and H₂O that take part, for example `MnO4- + Fe2+ + H+ -> Mn2+ + Fe3+ + H2O`; charges are balanced along with the atoms. Half-reactions with `e-` work too.

**What does “more than one balanced form” mean?**
Some equations combine two reactions that can happen in any proportion, such as `C + O2 -> CO + CO2`. They have endless valid sets of coefficients. The tool shows one small set and says so; split the equation into its separate reactions for a definite answer.

**How is the limiting reactant found?**
Each amount you enter is divided by that substance’s coefficient. The smallest result belongs to the limiting reactant — the one that runs out first — and it sets how much product forms. The table shows what is left of the other reactants.

**Which atomic weights are used?**
The abridged standard atomic weights from IUPAC’s Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (H 1.0080, C 12.011, O 15.999, and so on). Elements with no stable isotope use the mass number of their most stable isotope, and the tool notes that the result is approximate.

**Do I need to type the coefficients?**
No — leave them out. If you do type them, the tool tells you whether your version was already balanced, and replaces them if not.

**Does it show the steps?**
It shows the check that matters for marks: the count of each element, the charge and the mass on both sides. The coefficients themselves come from solving all the element equations at once, which is how the algebraic method taught in class works.

## Electron Configuration Builder

URL: https://justtools.info/education-tools/electron-configuration/
Category: Education Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-14

Electron Configuration Builder on Toolspire: Electron configuration of any element or ion: full and noble-gas form, orbital diagram.

### At a glance

- Electron Configuration Builder on Toolspire: gives the ground-state **electron configuration of all 118 elements**, in full (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ …) and in noble-gas shorthand ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²).
- Handles **ions from 4− to 8+**: electrons leave the outermost shell first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶, not [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
- Includes the **20 elements that break the filling order**, such as chromium ([Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹) and copper ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹), and shows what the rule would have predicted.
- Checked against the **NIST Atomic Spectra Database** for every atom from hydrogen to hassium and every positive ion of those elements up to 8+.
- Draws the **orbital diagram** with Hund’s rule, and can fill it one electron at a time.
- Lists electrons per shell, valence electrons, unpaired electrons, whether the atom is paramagnetic or diamagnetic, its block, period and group, and the **quantum numbers of the last electron**.
- **Practice mode**: fill the boxes yourself and get told which rule — Aufbau, Pauli or Hund — the first mistake breaks.
- Free, with nothing to install; works on a phone.

### Features

- **Atoms and ions**: Type Fe, iron, 26 or Fe3+, or click the periodic table and step the charge up and down.
- **Both ways of writing it**: By shell ([Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²), as most textbooks and data tables print it, or in filling order ([Ar] 4s² 3d⁶), as many classes teach it.
- **Exceptions explained**: For chromium, copper, silver, gold and the rest, the measured configuration is shown next to the predicted one, so you see exactly what differs.
- **A diagram you can build**: Click orbitals to add and pair electrons. The check points to the first subshell that is wrong and explains the rule behind it.
- **Answers the follow-up questions**: How many valence electrons? How many unpaired? Paramagnetic? What are n, l, mℓ and ms of the last electron? They are all on the page.
- **Backed by measured data**: Configurations follow NIST’s published ground states, not just a rule — including the awkward 1+ ions of vanadium, cobalt and nickel.

### How to find an electron configuration

1. **Choose the element** — Type a symbol, name or atomic number, or click the element in the periodic table.
2. **Set the charge** — For an ion, type it (Fe3+, Cl-) or use the − and + buttons beside the symbol.
3. **Read the configuration** — The noble-gas form and the full form appear with copy buttons. Switch the order between “by shell” and “as they fill” to match your course.
4. **Study the diagram** — The orbital diagram shows paired and unpaired electrons. Drag the slider to watch the orbitals fill one electron at a time.
5. **Practise** — Choose **Practice**, fill the boxes for the element shown and press **Check**.

### Guide

#### The three rules

- **Aufbau principle** — electrons fill the lowest-energy subshell that has room, in the order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.
- **Pauli exclusion principle** — an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. That makes the capacities s = 2, p = 6, d = 10, f = 14.
- **Hund’s rule** — within a subshell, every orbital gets one electron before any orbital gets a second.

#### Examples

| Atom or ion | Configuration | Unpaired electrons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon, C | [He] 2s² 2p² | 2 |
| Sodium, Na | [Ne] 3s¹ | 1 |
| Chlorine, Cl | [Ne] 3s² 3p⁵ | 1 |
| Iron, Fe | [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² | 4 |
| Chromium, Cr | [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (exception) | 6 |
| Copper, Cu | [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (exception) | 1 |
| Fe²⁺ | [Ar] 3d⁶ | 4 |
| Fe³⁺ | [Ar] 3d⁵ | 5 |
| Cu²⁺ | [Ar] 3d⁹ | 1 |
| Cl⁻ | [Ar] | 0 |

#### Elements that break the filling order

Twenty elements have a ground state the filling order does not predict: Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh, Pd, Ag, La, Ce, Gd, Pt, Au, Ac, Th, Pa, U, Np, Cm and Lr. In most of them an electron moves from the s subshell into d, because a half-filled or filled d subshell is slightly more stable — chromium is 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁴ 4s², and copper 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ rather than 3d⁹ 4s².

These cannot be worked out from the rule; they are measured. The tool shows the measured configuration and, beside it, what the rule alone would give.

#### Why ions lose 4s before 3d

In a neutral atom 4s fills before 3d. Once 3d holds electrons, though, it lies lower in energy than 4s, so when a transition metal becomes a positive ion the 4s electrons leave first. Iron, [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s², becomes Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Writing Fe²⁺ as [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s² — the configuration of a neutral atom with 24 electrons — is the commonest mistake, and Practice mode points it out.

### FAQ

**Where does Electron Configuration Builder run?**
Electron Configuration Builder runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**What is the electron configuration of iron?**
Iron (atomic number 26) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s², or [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² in short. It has 4 unpaired electrons. Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶ and Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.

**Should 4s or 3d be written first?**
Both are accepted. Writing by shell — [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² — is the convention of NIST and most reference tables. Writing in filling order — [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶ — is common in school courses. Use the switch under the result to match your textbook.

**How many valence electrons does an element have?**
For main-group elements (groups 1, 2 and 13–18) it is the number of s and p electrons in the outermost shell, and the tool shows it. For transition metals and the f-block the word has no single definition, because inner d or f electrons also take part in bonding, so the tool shows the outer-shell count and says so.

**What are the quantum numbers of the last electron?**
They describe the final electron added: n is its shell, l its subshell (0 = s, 1 = p, 2 = d, 3 = f), mℓ its orbital and ms its spin. The tool numbers orbitals from −l to +l and puts spin-up electrons in first, the convention most textbooks use; a few courses number them the other way round.

**Why is my answer for Cr or Cu marked wrong in Practice?**
Chromium and copper are exceptions: their ground states are 3d⁵ 4s¹ and 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. If you enter what the filling order predicts, the check tells you that it is the predicted configuration and what the real one is.

**How reliable are the configurations of the heaviest elements?**
From hydrogen to hassium (element 108) they are the ground states listed by NIST. For meitnerium to oganesson only a few atoms have ever been made, so the configurations are predictions from the filling order, and the tool labels them as such.

**Which ions can it show?**
Charges from 4− to 8+, which covers the ions met in chemistry. Positive ions follow NIST’s measured ground states; for negative ions the extra electrons are placed by the filling order.

### Guide

#### How Markdown maps to Notion blocks

| Markdown | Notion block | API type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `# Heading` to `#### Heading` | Heading 1 to 4 | `heading_1` … `heading_4` |
| `- item`, `1. item` | Bulleted or numbered list | `bulleted_list_item`, `numbered_list_item` |
| `- [ ] task`, `- [x] done` | To-do | `to_do` |
| `> quote` | Quote | `quote` |
| `> [!NOTE]` and other GitHub alerts | Callout | `callout` |
| `<details><summary>…</summary>` | Toggle | `toggle` |
| Fenced code with a language | Code | `code` |
| `$$ … $$` | Equation | `equation` |
| A table | Table | `table` with `table_row` children |
| `---` | Divider | `divider` |
| `![alt](https://…)` | Image | `image` (external) |
| `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `~~strike~~`, `` `code` ``, `[link](url)`, `$x$` | Text styles | rich text annotations, links and inline equations |

#### Which output to use

- **Copy for Notion** — for pasting by hand. It puts ordinary formatted text on the clipboard, as copying from a web page does. Notion-only blocks have no clipboard form, so a callout is pasted as a quote and an equation as code; the API outputs create the exact block.
- **API blocks (JSON)** — for code, Zapier, Make, n8n or any tool that calls the block endpoints. Use the *Append* body with `PATCH /v1/blocks/{id}/children`, or the *New page* body with `POST /v1/pages`.
- **Notion Markdown** — for the API’s newer `markdown` parameter. It is Notion’s “enhanced markdown”: tabs for nesting, `<callout>`, `<details>` and `<table>` tags, and Notion’s escaping rules. One request can create up to 5,000 blocks.

#### The limits it works within

| Limit in Notion’s API | What the tool does |
| --- | --- |
| 2,000 characters in one piece of text | Cuts longer text into pieces inside the same block |
| 100 items in any array | Continues a longer block in the next one; splits tables over 100 rows and repeats the heading row |
| 100 blocks per request | Writes several requests, to be sent in order |
| Two levels of nesting per request | Moves deeper blocks up a level and says how many |
| 1,000 blocks and 500 KB per request | Starts a new request before either is reached |
| 1,000 characters in an equation | Keeps a longer one as LaTeX code |

#### Good to know

- Notion only links to full web addresses. Fill in **Base address for relative links** to turn `./page.md` and `images/a.png` into complete URLs.
- Images must already be online at a public https:// address; the API reference lists .png, .jpg, .gif, .svg, .bmp, .heic and .tif for external images. Upload local images in Notion itself.
- Front matter at the top of a file is left out; its `title` becomes the page title for a new page. Otherwise the first `#` heading does.
- A line break inside a paragraph is a space, as in any Markdown renderer. End a line with two spaces or `<br>` for a real line break.
- Sending is optional. If you use it, your browser sends the blocks and your token straight to api.notion.com; this site has no server that could see them, and the token is forgotten when you close the page.

### FAQ

**Where does Markdown to Notion run?**
Markdown to Notion has to reach the network for a public lookup. The page says what leaves your device. Toolspire does not keep a copy of the query.

**How do I paste Markdown into Notion so it keeps its formatting?**
Paste the Markdown here, click **Copy for Notion** and paste into your page with Ctrl+V. The clipboard then holds the headings, lists, to-dos, tables, quotes and code as formatted text, the same as when you copy them from a web page. For callouts, toggles and equations exactly as written, send the page through the API instead.

**What is the “API blocks (JSON)” output for?**
Notion’s API builds pages from block objects. This output is that JSON — the `children` array — ready to send to `PATCH /v1/blocks/{page_id}/children` or `POST /v1/pages`, or to paste into the HTTP step of an automation tool.

**Why did my content come out as several requests?**
Notion accepts at most 100 blocks in one request. Longer documents are split into parts; send them in order, each to the same page. Use the arrows above the result to move between parts.

**What happens to lists nested many levels deep?**
One request can carry two levels of children. Blocks nested deeper are moved up to the second level, in the same order, and the note below the result says how many. The Notion Markdown output has no such limit.

**Can it send the page to Notion for me?**
Yes. Open **Send it to Notion from here**, paste a Notion token and choose a new page or an existing one. Your browser calls Notion’s API directly; the token is not saved anywhere. If you would rather not paste a token into a web page, copy the JSON and send it yourself.

**Does it work with ChatGPT or Claude output?**
Yes — that is a common use. Copy the answer as Markdown and paste it here. Tables, nested lists, code and maths written as `\( … \)` or `\[ … \]` are converted to Notion tables, lists, code blocks and equations.

**Which Notion API version does the JSON follow?**
Version 2026-03-11, the current one when this tool was written, which added a fourth heading level. If your tool only knows three, set **Heading levels** to *Up to 3* under Options.

**Where do I get a Notion token?**
In Notion’s developer portal, under Personal access tokens: create a token with the Notion API capability and copy it. With such a token, leaving the parent page blank creates a private page in your workspace. A token from an internal connection also works, after you add that connection to the page under ••• → Connections.

**Is my text uploaded?**
Not unless you press Send. The conversion runs in this tab, and this site has no server that receives your text. When you do send, the blocks go from your browser to Notion and nowhere else.

## Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker

URL: https://justtools.info/seo-tools/dofollow-nofollow-checker/

Last updated: 2026-10-14

Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker on Toolspire: See which links on a page are dofollow or nofollow. Lists every link with its rel, anchor text and type.

### At a glance

- Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker on Toolspire: lists **every link on a page** and labels each as followed (dofollow), **nofollow**, **sponsored** or **UGC**, with its anchor text, address and rel values.
- Counts followed and nofollow links, internal and external links, different addresses and the outside sites linked to.
- Checks a **backlink**: type your domain to see each link the page gives you and whether it is followed.
- Reads the page’s robots meta tag: `<meta name="robots" content="nofollow">` makes every link on the page nofollow, and the tool counts them so.
- Treats `sponsored` and `ugc` like `nofollow`, as Google does — links with any of the three “will generally not be followed”.
- Warns about nofollow on your own internal links, links with no anchor text, and the meaningless `rel="dofollow"`.
- Works from a page address or from **pasted HTML** — useful for pages behind a login. Pasted HTML never leaves your device.
- Filter, search, copy the addresses or download the list as CSV.

### Features

- **Every link, one table**: Anchor text, full address, rel values, internal or external, the part of the page it sits in and whether it opens a new tab.
- **Backlink check in one step**: Paid for a guest post or earned a mention? Enter the page and your domain to confirm the link is there and is followed.
- **Page-wide rules included**: A robots meta tag can make a whole page nofollow without touching any link. The tool reads it, which a look at single links misses.
- **JavaScript pages too**: Turn on **Run JavaScript first** for sites that build their links in the browser, such as React or Vue apps.
- **Export**: Copy the addresses of the links you have filtered, or download them as a CSV file for a spreadsheet.
- **Careful with your data**: Only the page address is sent out to fetch the page. HTML you paste is read in this tab and goes nowhere.

### How to check dofollow and nofollow links

1. **Enter the page** — Type or paste the address of the page whose links you want to see, and click **Check links**.
2. **Read the summary** — The tiles show how many links are followed and nofollow, and how many go to other sites.
3. **Check a backlink** — Type your own domain under **Does this page link to your site?** to see the links to it and their type.
4. **Filter the list** — Show only nofollow links, only external ones, or search for a word or address.
5. **Export** — Click **Copy addresses** or **CSV** to take the filtered list with you.

### Guide

#### What the rel values mean

| In the link | Shown as | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no rel, or only `noopener`, `noreferrer`, `external` | Followed | An ordinary link. Search engines may follow it and count it as a vote for the page it points to. |
| `rel="nofollow"` | Nofollow | The site does not want to be associated with the linked page, or have it crawled from here. |
| `rel="sponsored"` | Sponsored | An advertisement or paid placement. Google’s preferred value for paid links. |
| `rel="ugc"` | UGC | User-generated content, such as comments and forum posts. |
| `rel="ugc nofollow"` | Nofollow + UGC | Values can be combined, separated by spaces or commas. |
| `<meta name="robots" content="nofollow">` in the page | Nofollow (page) | Every link on the page is nofollow, whatever its own rel. |

#### There is no “dofollow” attribute

“Dofollow” is only a name for a normal link — one without `nofollow`, `sponsored` or `ugc`. Links are followed by default, so nothing needs to be added. Writing `rel="dofollow"` does nothing; if a page uses it, the tool says so.

Since 2019 Google has treated `nofollow`, `sponsored` and `ugc` as hints rather than strict orders: such links will generally not be followed, but Google may choose to use them. Other search engines make their own choices.

#### What counts as a link here

- Links to web pages — `<a href>` and image-map `<area href>` — are counted and labelled.
- Jumps within the same page (`#section`), e-mail and phone links and `javascript:` links do not lead to another page. They are listed under **Not pages** and left out of the counts.
- A link to the same site with or without `www.` is internal. Links to other subdomains, such as blog.example.com from example.com, count as external.
- Links inside `<noscript>` and `<template>` are ignored, as they are not part of the page a visitor sees.

#### What it cannot see

- Links added by JavaScript after the page loads, unless **Run JavaScript first** is on.
- A nofollow sent as an `X-Robots-Tag` HTTP header. Browsers do not let one website read another’s headers.
- Pages behind a login, or sites that block automated visitors. Open the page yourself, copy its source (Ctrl+U) and use **Paste HTML**.
- Whether a search engine really followed a link. The tool reports what the page asks for.

### FAQ

**Where does Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker run?**
Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker has to reach the network for a public lookup. The page says what leaves your device. Toolspire does not keep a copy of the query.

**What is the difference between dofollow and nofollow links?**
A dofollow link is a normal link: search engines can follow it and treat it as a recommendation of the page it points to. A nofollow link carries `rel="nofollow"` (or `sponsored` or `ugc`), which asks search engines not to follow it or pass ranking credit through it.

**How do I check if a backlink is dofollow?**
Enter the address of the page that links to you and click **Check links**. Then type your domain in the backlink box. The tool lists each link to your site and labels it Followed, Nofollow, Sponsored or UGC.

**Are sponsored and UGC links nofollow?**
In effect, yes. Google introduced `sponsored` for paid links and `ugc` for user-generated content in 2019, and says links marked with any of the three values will generally not be followed. The tool counts all three as nofollow and shows which value each link uses.

**Why does the tool say all links are nofollow when they have no rel?**
The page has a robots meta tag with `nofollow` (or `none`). That applies to every link on the page at once. The tool shows the tag and marks such links “Nofollow (page)”.

**Should my internal links be nofollow?**
Usually not. Links between your own pages help search engines discover them and understand which matter most. The tool flags internal links that carry nofollow so you can decide.

**Where does the page get fetched from?**
Your browser asks the website directly. Most sites do not allow one website to read another, so the address is then sent to Jina Reader (r.jina.ai), which fetches the page. Only the address is sent. To avoid that, paste the HTML instead.

**Why are some links missing?**
They are probably added by JavaScript. Turn on **Run JavaScript first** and check again, or open the page, copy the HTML from your browser’s developer tools and paste it.

2. **Choose a background** — Try the built-in backgrounds, or **Use your own photo** — a screenshot of the page where the glass will sit is best.

### Guide

#### What glassmorphism is

Glassmorphism is a style of interface where cards, menus and panels look like frosted glass: you can see colours and shapes behind them, softly blurred, while text on top stays sharp. Apple uses it across macOS and iOS, Windows calls its version acrylic, and it became a web design trend in 2020.

In CSS the effect comes from one property, `backdrop-filter`, which blurs whatever is behind an element. It only shows when the element’s own background is partly transparent — a solid background hides the blur completely.

#### The CSS behind the effect

| Property | Typical value | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `background` | `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.25)` | the tint: a see-through colour; lower opacity shows more of the background |
| `backdrop-filter` | `blur(16px) saturate(180%)` | blurs what is behind; saturation above 100% makes those colours richer |
| `-webkit-backdrop-filter` | the same | the same, for Safari before version 18 |
| `border` | `1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45)` | a light edge that separates the glass from the background |
| `box-shadow` | `0 6px 21px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.14)` | lifts the card; an inset line can add a bright top edge |
| `border-radius` | `24px` | rounded corners, typical of glass surfaces |

#### Keeping text readable on glass

Text on glass sits on a background that changes from place to place, so it can be readable in one corner and not in another. WCAG 2 asks for a contrast of at least **4.5:1** for normal text and **3:1** for large text. This tool measures the glass over the whole card and reports the weakest spot.

If text is hard to read, raise the tint opacity, blur more (which evens out the background), switch between dark and light text, or give the text its own slightly darker or lighter panel.

#### Browser support

Figures from MDN’s browser compatibility data, October 2026. Browsers without the media query simply ignore it, so the fallback is safe to keep.

| Browser | backdrop-filter | prefers-reduced-transparency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chrome and Edge | since version 76 | since version 118 |
| Firefox | since version 103 | behind a setting only |
| Safari (macOS and iOS) | since 18; with `-webkit-` since 9 | not supported |

### FAQ

**Where does CSS Glassmorphism Generator run?**
CSS Glassmorphism Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Why does my backdrop-filter blur not show?**
Usually because the element’s background is solid — the blur is behind it, so make the background partly transparent. Also check that there is something behind the element to blur. If a parent element has its own filter, opacity below 1, a mask or a backdrop-filter, the specification says the blur only sees what is inside that parent (it calls this the backdrop root).

**Do I still need -webkit-backdrop-filter?**
Only for Safari 17 and older, which understood the prefixed name only. Safari 18 and every current Chrome, Edge and Firefox read `backdrop-filter`. Keeping both lines costs nothing, so the tool writes both.

**How do I make glassmorphism in Tailwind CSS?**
Use a semi-transparent background, a backdrop blur and a light border, for example `bg-white/25 backdrop-blur-lg backdrop-saturate-180 border border-white/45 rounded-3xl`. Open the **Tailwind** tab to get the classes for your exact settings.

**Is glassmorphism bad for performance?**
backdrop-filter makes the browser redraw what is behind the element whenever it changes, which costs more on large areas, big blur values and older phones. Use it on cards, menus and dialogs rather than whole pages, and avoid stacking many glass layers on top of each other.

**What is the difference between glassmorphism and neumorphism?**
Glassmorphism is see-through: a blurred view of what is behind. Neumorphism is solid: soft light and dark shadows make an element look pressed out of, or into, the same coloured surface. Try the [CSS Neumorphism Generator](https://justtools.info/css-tools/neumorphism-generator/) for that look.

**What does “Reduce transparency” do with my glass?**
Some people switch on Reduce transparency because see-through surfaces are tiring or hard to read. With **Add fallbacks** on, the CSS gives them a solid surface through the `prefers-reduced-transparency` media query, in a colour that keeps your text readable.

**Can it make Apple’s “Liquid Glass” look?**
Not the bending of light at the edges: that needs an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter, which for now works only in Chromium browsers such as Chrome and Edge. This tool makes the frosted glass that works in every current browser, and the bright top edge and sheen give some of the same feel.

**Is my photo uploaded?**
No. The photo is read by your browser to show it behind the glass and to measure contrast, and it is never sent anywhere or saved. Your slider settings are kept in this browser’s local storage only.

## CSS Neumorphism Generator

URL: https://justtools.info/css-tools/neumorphism-generator/

Last updated: 2026-10-14

CSS Neumorphism Generator on Toolspire: Neumorphism generator: soft UI box-shadows from any colour and light angle, with contrast checks, pressed states.

### At a glance

- CSS Neumorphism Generator on Toolspire: writes the two `box-shadow`s of neumorphism — a light one towards the light and a dark one away from it — for **flat, concave, convex and pressed** shapes.
- The light can come from **any angle**, not just the four corners; drag on the preview to move it.

- Measures how visible the element’s edge is. Soft shadows alone usually reach well under the **3:1** that WCAG 2.1 (success criterion 1.4.11) asks for buttons and inputs, so one click adds a border that passes.
- Optional **button states**: a pressed-in shadow while clicked, a focus ring for keyboard users, and a `forced-colors` border so the shape survives Windows High Contrast, which removes shadows.

- **Any light direction**: Choose one of eight directions or any angle from 0° to 359°. The shadows, the convex gradient and the pressed look all follow the light.
- **Accessible soft UI**: Neumorphism is known for low contrast. The tool tells you the edge and text contrast and fixes them for you, instead of hiding the problem.

### How to make a neumorphism effect in CSS

1. **Choose the surface colour** — Pick the colour of the page behind your element — the element uses the same colour. Light greys such as `#e0e5ec` give the classic look; dark surfaces work too.
2. **Choose the shape** — **Flat** and **Convex** look pressed out, **Concave** looks scooped, **Pressed** looks pushed in.
3. **Set the light** — Click a direction or drag on the preview. Then adjust **Distance**, **Blur** and **Intensity** — a blur about twice the distance looks softest.
4. **Check the edges** — Read the checks under the preview. Switch on **Visible edge** for buttons and inputs, and use the suggested text colour if yours is too faint.
5. **Copy the code** — Copy the **CSS** or **Tailwind** classes for one element, or the **UI kit** for a full set of controls.

### Guide

#### How neumorphism works

Neumorphism (new skeuomorphism, or soft UI) makes elements look moulded from the background itself. The element has the same colour as the surface behind it, and two shadows shape it: a dark one on the side away from the light and a light one on the side facing it.

In CSS that is a single `box-shadow` with two values, such as `16px 16px 32px #bfc3ca, -16px -16px 32px #ffffff`. The word `inset` in front of both turns the shape into a hollow; a gradient background makes it convex or concave.

#### The four shapes

| Shape | Background | Shadow | Looks like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flat | the surface colour | outside | a raised, flat-topped tile |
| Convex | gradient, light side lighter | outside | a domed button |
| Concave | gradient, light side darker | outside | a raised dish |
| Pressed | the surface colour | inset | a hole or a pushed-in button |

#### Making neumorphism accessible

- WCAG 2.1 asks for **3:1** contrast for the visual boundary of buttons, inputs and other controls (success criterion 1.4.11). Soft shadows rarely reach it, so add a border to anything people must find and use — **Visible edge** does this with a colour that passes.
- Text needs **4.5:1** against the surface (3:1 for large text). Grey-on-grey text is the most common neumorphism mistake.
- Do not rely on the pressed look alone to show that a toggle is on; add a label, an icon or a colour change.
- Windows High Contrast mode removes box-shadows. The CSS adds a border inside `@media (forced-colors: active)` so every element still has an outline.
- Keep a visible focus ring for keyboard users; the tool’s button states include one.

### FAQ

**Where does CSS Neumorphism Generator run?**
CSS Neumorphism Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Why does neumorphism not work on a white background?**
The light shadow has to be lighter than the surface, and nothing is lighter than white — so the top edge disappears. Use a light grey such as `#e0e5ec` or `#f0f0f3` instead; the tool warns you when the surface is too light or too dark.

**How do I make a neumorphic button pressed when clicked?**
Give the button an inset version of its shadow in `:active`, for example `.neu:active { box-shadow: inset 9.6px 9.6px 19.2px #bfc3ca, inset -9.6px -9.6px 19.2px #ffffff; }`. With **Button states** on, the tool writes this for you, plus a focus ring and a smooth transition.

**How do I do neumorphism in Tailwind CSS?**
Use arbitrary values: a background the same as the page, such as `bg-[#e0e5ec]`, and a shadow like `shadow-[16px_16px_32px_#bfc3ca,-16px_-16px_32px_#ffffff]`. The **Tailwind** tab gives you the exact classes for your settings, including `active:` and `focus-visible:` states.

**Can neumorphism work in dark mode?**
Yes. Choose a dark surface such as `#2b2f36` and raise the intensity a little, because shadows show less on dark colours. Use light text and check its contrast in the panel under the preview.

**Is neumorphism bad for accessibility?**
It can be, because the shapes are drawn only with subtle shadows. It works when you add a visible border to controls, keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more, and never use the pressed look as the only sign of state. The tool checks the first two for you.

**What is the difference between concave and convex?**
Both are raised from the surface. Convex has a gradient that is lighter on the side facing the light, so it bulges like a dome; concave has the opposite gradient, so it looks like a shallow dish.

**Are my settings saved?**
They are kept in this browser’s local storage so they are still there next time. Nothing is uploaded.

### Guide

#### What a bento grid is

A bento grid arranges content in tiles of different sizes inside one rectangle, like the compartments of a Japanese bento lunch box. A large tile carries the main message and smaller ones hold details, stats or images. Apple’s product pages made the style popular, and it now appears on portfolios, landing pages and dashboards.

CSS Grid is made for it: one container with `display: grid`, columns of equal width, and each tile told how many columns and rows to span.

#### How the generated CSS works

`grid-auto-rows: minmax(…, auto)` gives every row a minimum height but lets it grow when a tile has more content, so text is never cut off.

| Screen | Columns | How tiles are placed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phone (under 640 px) | your phone setting, usually 1 | one after another in reading order; tall tiles keep their height |
| Tablet (640–1023 px) | your tablet setting, usually 2 | spans shrunk to fit, in reading order |
| Desktop (1024 px and up) | as drawn | exactly where you drew them, with `grid-template-areas` or line numbers |

#### Bento layouts that work for everyone

- Keep the HTML in the order people should read it. This tool writes tiles left to right, top to bottom, exactly as you see them on desktop.
- `grid-auto-flow: dense` fills holes by moving later tiles up. That can make the order on screen differ from the order a keyboard or screen reader follows — fine for pictures, not for links and buttons.
- Put the most important content in the biggest tile; it is also the first tile on phones.
- Give tiles enough contrast with the page background, and let text wrap instead of fixing tile heights.

### FAQ

**Where does Bento Grid Generator run?**
Bento Grid Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**How do I make a bento grid in CSS?**
Use a grid container, for example `display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: 16px;`, then give big tiles a span such as `grid-column: span 2; grid-row: span 2;`. Draw your layout here and the tool writes all of this, plus the rules for tablets and phones.

**What is grid-template-areas?**
A CSS property that lets you draw the layout in text: each quoted string is a row and each word is a cell, so `"hero hero stats"` puts the hero tile across two columns. A dot marks an empty cell. Each tile then gets `grid-area: hero;`.

**How do I make a bento grid with Tailwind CSS?**
Use `grid` with responsive column counts such as `grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4`, a row height like `auto-rows-[minmax(180px,auto)]`, and spans on the tiles such as `row-span-2 sm:col-span-2`. The **Tailwind** tab gives you the exact classes for your layout.

**How does the layout change on mobile?**
On phones the tiles stack in reading order in the number of columns you choose (one by default). On tablets, wide tiles shrink to fit the tablet columns. Open the **Phone** and **Tablet** views to see it before you copy the code.

**Why are there holes in my tablet layout?**
In reading order, a wide tile sometimes cannot fit next to the tile before it, so it starts a new row and leaves a gap. Change the tile sizes or the tablet columns, or switch on **Fill holes on smaller screens**, which lets later tiles move up into the gaps.

**Can I edit the grid with a keyboard?**
Yes. Press Tab to reach a tile, then use the arrow keys to move it, Shift with the arrow keys to resize it, and Delete to remove it. **Add tile** puts a new tile in the first free cell.

**Is my layout saved?**
Yes, in this browser’s local storage, so it is still there when you come back. Nothing is uploaded.
