- **Solid, liquid or gas**: Slide the temperature from absolute zero to the surface of the Sun and watch elements melt and boil. Carbon and arsenic sublime; helium never freezes at normal pressure.
- **Search that understands families**: Type “halogens”, “noble gases”, “group 2”, “period 4” or “f-block” to light up a whole family, or a name, symbol or number to jump to one element.
- **Learn it by heart**: Three quiz types and six ranges, from the first 20 elements to the full table. Hard mode hides every symbol so you find elements from their place alone.
- **Print a clean copy**: A sharp vector PDF that prints at true size, with numbers, symbols, names and atomic weights — or blank for practice. Colour or black and white.

### How to use the periodic table

1. **Find an element** — Click it in the table, or type its name, symbol or atomic number in the search box and press Enter.
2. **Read its properties** — The card under the table lists its configuration, shells, oxidation states, electronegativity, radius, energies, melting and boiling points and density. Use the arrows to step to the next element.
3. **Colour the table** — Pick **Colour by** — family, block, metals and nonmetals, state of matter, or a property heat map. Point at a legend entry to light up that group.
4. **Change the temperature** — In the state-of-matter view, drag the slider or pick a preset such as body temperature to see what melts and boils.
5. **Quiz yourself or print** — Choose **Quiz** to practise, or **Print & download** for a PDF, PNG or SVG of the table.

### Guide

#### How the periodic table is arranged

Elements are placed in order of **atomic number** — the number of protons — in 7 rows called **periods** and 18 columns called **groups**. Elements in the same group have the same arrangement of outer electrons, which is why they behave alike: the alkali metals in group 1 all react with water, the halogens in group 17 all form salts, the noble gases in group 18 hardly react at all.

The table splits into **blocks** named after the subshell being filled: the s-block (groups 1–2 and helium), the p-block (groups 13–18), the d-block (groups 3–12, the transition metals) and the f-block (the two rows shown underneath, which would make the table 32 columns wide if fitted in).

This table puts **lutetium and lawrencium in group 3**, under scandium and yttrium, and the 14 elements from lanthanum to ytterbium and from actinium to nobelium in the f-block rows — the layout an IUPAC project report favoured in 2021. Many textbooks, including NCERT’s, put lanthanum and actinium in group 3 instead; the elements and their properties are the same either way.

#### Periodic trends at a glance

Trends have exceptions — nitrogen’s ionisation energy is higher than oxygen’s, and fluorine’s electron affinity is lower than chlorine’s — so the heat maps and the trend chart are worth a look rather than relying on the rule alone.

| Property | Across a period (left → right) | Down a group | Highest |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Atomic radius | Decreases | Increases | Francium (348 pm, van der Waals) |
| Electronegativity | Increases | Decreases | Fluorine (3.98) |
| First ionisation energy | Increases | Decreases | Helium (24.587 eV) |
| Electron affinity | Generally increases | Generally decreases | Chlorine (3.617 eV) |
| Metallic character | Decreases | Increases | Caesium and francium |

#### Where the data come from

- Names and **atomic weights**: IUPAC and its Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights (CIAAW, 2021 abridged values).
- **Electron configurations**: built by the same engine as our [Electron Configuration Builder](https://justtools.info/education-tools/electron-configuration/), which is checked against the NIST Atomic Spectra Database.
- **Electronegativity, radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity, oxidation states, melting and boiling points, density and families**: PubChem’s periodic table (US National Library of Medicine), compiled from Jefferson Lab and Los Alamos National Laboratory. Three values are corrected: helium has no melting point at normal pressure, and carbon and arsenic sublime instead of melting.
- Astatine, francium and the elements from fermium (100) on have never been made in a visible amount, so their physical values are estimates; from meitnerium (109) on, even the chemistry is a prediction. The page says so wherever it shows them.

#### The first 20 elements

Many school syllabuses ask for the first 20 (or 30) elements by heart. In order: hydrogen (H), helium (He), lithium (Li), beryllium (Be), boron (B), carbon (C), nitrogen (N), oxygen (O), fluorine (F), neon (Ne), sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), aluminium (Al), silicon (Si), phosphorus (P), sulfur (S), chlorine (Cl), argon (Ar), potassium (K) and calcium (Ca). Use the quiz with **First 20** to practise them until they stick.

### FAQ

**Where does Interactive Periodic Table run?**

**How many elements are in the periodic table?**
118. The last four — nihonium (113), moscovium (115), tennessine (117) and oganesson (118) — were named in 2016, completing the seventh period.

**Why are some atomic weights in square brackets?**
Those elements have no stable isotope, so they have no standard atomic weight. The number in brackets is the mass number of the longest-lived isotope, e.g. [97] for technetium.

**Which elements are liquid at room temperature?**
At 25 °C only **bromine** and **mercury**. Gallium (29.8 °C), caesium (28.4 °C) and rubidium (39.3 °C) melt just above it — set the state-of-matter slider to body temperature and gallium and caesium turn liquid.

**Where do the lanthanides and actinides go?**
In the two rows under the main table. They belong between groups 2 and 3 but would make the table 32 columns wide, so they are printed separately. This table puts lutetium and lawrencium in group 3; some books put lanthanum and actinium there.

**What do the colours mean?**
In the default view each colour is a family: alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, transition metals, post-transition metals, metalloids, nonmetals, halogens, noble gases, lanthanides and actinides. Point at a legend entry to light up its members. Other views colour by block, by metal type, by state or by the size of a property.

**Can I print the periodic table?**
Yes. Choose **Print & download**, pick the paper (A4, Letter, A3 or Tabloid), colour or black and white, and what each box shows — full details, symbols, numbers only or blank. Print it directly, or download a PDF, PNG or SVG. Keep the scale at 100% when printing the PDF.

**Is the electron configuration shown measured or predicted?**
For elements up to hassium (108) it matches NIST’s measured ground states, including exceptions such as chromium ([Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹) and copper ([Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹). Beyond that the configurations come from theory.

**Does it work offline?**
Yes. Everything — data, quiz and PDF — runs in this tab. Settings and quiz best scores are saved on your device only.

### How to build a layout with flexbox or grid

1. **Pick Flexbox or Grid** — Flexbox lays items out in one direction (a row or a column); grid places them in rows and columns at once. Or start from one of the examples.
2. **Set the container** — Click values such as justify-content: space-between or grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) and watch the preview.
3. **Adjust single items** — Click an item, then give it flex-grow, a fixed flex-basis, its own alignment, or grid lines and spans. In grid mode you can drag its area on the grid.
4. **Test it** — Drag the container width slider to see how the layout responds on narrow screens.
5. **Copy the code** — Choose CSS, HTML, Tailwind or React, then Copy or Download. Share builds a link to this exact layout.

### Guide

#### Flexbox or grid?

**Flexbox** is for laying things out along one line — a navigation bar, a row of buttons, a card’s header and footer — where the content decides the sizes and items may wrap. **Grid** is for two-dimensional layouts — page structure, galleries, dashboards — where you define the columns and rows first and place items into them.

They work well together: a grid for the page, flexbox inside each card.

#### The properties people mix up

In flexbox, switching flex-direction to column swaps the axes: justify-content then works vertically and align-items horizontally. justify-items does nothing in flexbox.

| Property | Works along | What it moves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| justify-content | Main axis (flex) / inline axis (grid) | The items as a group (flex) or the whole set of tracks (grid) |
| align-items | Cross axis (flex) / block axis (grid) | Each item inside its line or grid area |
| align-content | Cross axis | Whole lines of wrapped items (flex) or rows of tracks (grid) |
| justify-items | Inline axis (grid only) | Each item inside its grid area |
| align-self / justify-self | Same as align-items / justify-items | One item, overriding the container |

#### flex-grow, flex-shrink and flex-basis

- **flex-basis** is the starting size along the main axis. `auto` uses the item’s width (or its content); `0` ignores content so space is shared purely by flex-grow.
- **flex-grow** shares out leftover space: an item with 2 gets twice as much of the extra as an item with 1. With 0 it never grows.
- **flex-shrink** decides who gives up space when there is not enough; 0 means the item never shrinks below its basis.
- The shorthand `flex: 1` means `1 1 0%`; `flex: auto` means `1 1 auto`; `flex: none` means `0 0 auto`. This tool always writes all three values so nothing is hidden.

#### auto-fill vs auto-fit

`repeat(auto-fill, minmax(140px, 1fr))` makes as many 140px-or-wider columns as fit, keeping empty columns when there are few items. `auto-fit` does the same but collapses empty columns, so a few items stretch across the full width. Load the **Responsive cards** example, remove items and switch between the two to see the difference.

### FAQ

**Where does CSS Flexbox & Grid Playground run?**
CSS Flexbox & Grid Playground runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**What is the difference between justify-content and align-items?**
justify-content distributes items along the main axis (left to right in a row); align-items positions them on the cross axis (top to bottom in a row). Switch flex-direction to column and they swap directions.

**Why does align-content do nothing?**
In flexbox it only affects containers whose items wrap onto more than one line — set flex-wrap: wrap and give the container some height. In grid it moves the rows when they are shorter than the container.

**Why does my flex item not shrink below its text?**
Flex items have a default min-width of auto, so they will not shrink below their longest word or a fixed-size child. Add min-width: 0 to the item (min-w-0 in Tailwind) to let it shrink.

**What does 1fr mean in CSS grid?**
One fraction of the leftover space. In grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr, the second column gets twice the free space of the first. Note that 1fr has a minimum of auto, so long content can widen it; minmax(0, 1fr) — what Tailwind’s grid-cols-3 uses — prevents that.

**Is the Tailwind code for Tailwind v3 or v4?**
Tailwind CSS v4. Most classes are the same in v3, but v4 accepts any spacing step (gap-13, basis-30); in v3 use an arbitrary value such as gap-[52px] for steps the default scale lacks.

**Can I use gap with flexbox?**
Yes — in Chrome 84+, Edge 84+, Firefox 63+ and Safari 14.1+. For much older browsers use margins on the items instead.

**Does order change the reading order?**
No. order, row-reverse, column-reverse and grid placement change only what you see. Screen readers and keyboard focus follow the HTML, so the tool warns you when the two may differ.

**Is my layout saved?**
Yes, in this tab on this device. Use Share to copy a link that opens the same layout anywhere — it is stored in the link itself, not on a server.

### Guide

#### ID card sizes

| Size | Millimetres | Inches | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

#### Printing on paper

- Print at **100% / Actual size**. “Fit to page” shrinks the cards slightly, so they no longer fit standard holders.

### Guide

#### What a Luxembourg invoice must show

Article 63 §8 of the VAT law lists the details; the company law of 10 August 1915 adds the identification of companies. This tool prints all of them:

- The **date of issue** and a **unique sequential number**, which may follow one or more series.
- Your **VAT number**, and the **customer’s VAT number** when they account for the VAT (reverse charge) or receive an intra-Community supply of goods.
- The **full name and address** of both parties.
- The **quantity and nature** of the goods or the **extent and nature** of the services, and the **date of supply** if it differs from the invoice date.
- The **taxable amount for each rate** or exemption, the **unit price excluding VAT**, discounts, the **rate** and the **VAT due**.
- For an exemption, the **legal reference**; for reverse charge, **“Autoliquidation”**; with cash accounting, **“Comptabilité de caisse”**.
- For a company: its name with the **legal form** (SA, SARL…), the **registered office** and **“R.C.S. Luxembourg”** with its registration number.

#### Luxembourg VAT rates

Which rate applies depends on the annexes of the VAT law and its regulations — check with the AED (Administration de l’enregistrement, des domaines et de la TVA) if you are not sure for a given product.

| Rate | Name | Typical uses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 17 % | Normal rate | Most goods and services |
| 14 % | Intermediate rate | Wines up to 13 % alcohol, mineral fuels and heating oil, washing and cleaning products, advertising print, custody of securities (annex C) |
| 8 % | Reduced rate | Gas, electricity, district heating, firewood, hairdressing, repairs of shoes, clothes and household appliances, bicycles (annex A) |
| 3 % | Super-reduced rate | Food (not alcoholic drinks), books and newspapers, children’s clothes, medicines, restaurant meals (not alcohol), hotels, passenger transport, entry to culture and sport (annex B) |

#### Small businesses: the VAT franchise

Businesses established in Luxembourg whose annual turnover in Luxembourg does not exceed **€50,000** (the threshold since 1 January 2025) can use the franchise: they charge no VAT and cannot deduct it. If turnover passes €50,000 the exemption continues until the end of the year as long as it stays within €55,000; above that it ends the next day (AED SME scheme FAQ).

Franchise invoices may not show VAT and must carry the statement “TVA non applicable – Article 57bis de la loi modifiée du 12 février 1979”. Since 2025 they may also be simplified invoices.

#### E-invoicing in Luxembourg

Invoices to Luxembourg **public bodies** must be electronic, in the European standard EN 16931 sent over Peppol — for all suppliers since 18 March 2023. The **e-invoice (UBL)** button makes such a file; send it through a Peppol access point or the State’s e-invoicing service.

For **business-to-business** invoices, a government bill (n° 8815, filed in July 2026) proposes compulsory e-invoicing from 2028 for receiving and from 2028–2029 for issuing. It is still a draft; until it becomes law, PDF invoices remain fine between businesses.

### FAQ

**Where does Luxembourg Invoice Generator run?**
Luxembourg Invoice Generator runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Do I have to write my invoice in French?**
No. Invoices can be in any language, but the AED may ask for a French or German translation of invoices in another language (art. 63 §12). French, German and English — or bilingual — are built in.

**When must an invoice be issued?**
At the latest on the 15th day of the month after the month of the supply, and for an advance payment at the latest when you receive it (art. 63 §5). The checklist warns you when the invoice date is later.

**What do I write for a customer in another EU country?**
For services to a business, no Luxembourg VAT is charged and the invoice says “Autoliquidation” (reverse charge), with the customer’s VAT number. For goods shipped to a VAT-registered business in another EU country, the supply is exempt (art. 43 §1 d) and the invoice says so. Choose the matching regime and the wording is added.

**I am a freelancer under the franchise. What goes on my invoice?**
No VAT, and the statement “TVA non applicable – Article 57bis de la loi modifiée du 12 février 1979”. Switch on “I use the VAT franchise” and the tool does the rest.

**Is an RCS number required on invoices?**
For commercial companies, yes: the 1915 company law requires the name, legal form, registered office and “R.C.S. Luxembourg” followed by the registration number on invoices and letters.

**What is a simplified invoice?**
An invoice with fewer details, allowed when the total including VAT is no more than €100, for documents that amend an earlier invoice, and for businesses under the franchise (art. 63 §10–11). This tool always produces a full invoice, which is valid in every case.

**Does the SEPA QR code work with my bank?**
It follows the European Payments Council standard (EPC069-12, also called GiroCode). Many banking apps in the euro area can read it; if a customer’s app cannot, the IBAN and reference are printed beside it.

**Is my data uploaded?**
No. The invoice is built in this tab. Your business details, logo and customers are saved on this device only, so they are there next time.

## Connect Four

URL: https://justtools.info/games/connect-four/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-20

Connect Four on Toolspire: Play Connect Four here: drop discs and get four in a row against the computer — Easy, Medium or Hard — or a friend on one device.

### At a glance

- Connect Four on Toolspire: the classic **7-column, 6-row** board, plus larger **8×7** and **9×7** boards for a longer game.
- Play the computer on **Easy, Medium or Hard**, or a friend taking turns on the same phone, tablet or computer.
- Hard searches many moves ahead — with alpha-beta pruning and a transposition table — for up to a second per move and never misses a win or a block it can see.
- Connect Four is a **solved game**: with perfect play the first player wins by starting in the centre column, at the latest on the 41st move. James D. Allen and Victor Allis proved it independently in October 1988.
- The 7×6 board has **4,531,985,219,092** possible positions.
- Hints, undo, sound, full screen and keyboard play (keys 1–7 drop a disc); scores are kept on your device. Free, with no download or sign-up.

### Features

- **An opponent for everyone**: Easy for children, Medium for a fair game and Hard for a real challenge — it blocks threats and sets up its own.
- **Two players, one screen**: Pass the phone or share the keyboard, with your own names and a running score.
- **Learn the tricks**: Ask for a hint to see the strongest column — it tells you when a forced win is on the board.
- **Fair starts**: Turn on “Take turns going first” so the first move swaps every game — going first is a real advantage.
- **Bigger boards**: Try 8×7 or 9×7 for more room to build threats.
- **Plays anywhere**: Phones, tablets and computers, with keyboard control and screen-reader announcements of every move.

### How to play Connect Four

1. **Pick an opponent** — Choose **Computer** and a difficulty, and your colour — Red moves first — or **A friend** to play on the same device.
2. **Drop a disc** — Tap a column (or press its number). The disc falls to the lowest free space.
3. **Make four in a row** — Line up four of your discs across, down or diagonally before your opponent does. A full board with no line is a draw.
4. **Play again** — Press **Play again** — the score keeps adding up. Use **Hint** or **Undo** while you learn.

### Guide

#### Connect Four strategy

- **Take the centre.** The middle column is part of more possible lines than any other — that is why perfect play starts there.
- **Block threes at once.** If your opponent has three in a row with an empty square they can reach, drop there before anything else.
- **Build double threats.** Two winning squares at the same time can’t both be blocked — the most common way games are won.
- **Watch the square below.** Don’t fill the space directly under your opponent’s winning square: your disc lets theirs land on it.
- **Think in rows.** The first player usually wants threats on odd rows (counting from the bottom), the second player on even rows — a key idea in Victor Allis’s solution.

#### How the computer plays

The computer reads the board column by column, tries the centre first and looks ahead with a minimax search pruned by alpha-beta, remembering positions it has already scored. When it can’t see to the end of the game it scores the board by the open lines each side still has. Hard thinks for up to a second and often looks ten or more moves ahead; it is strong, but it is not a perfect solver — a well-built trap can still beat it.

**Who wins Connect Four with perfect play?**
The first player. Starting in the middle column, the first player can always force a win — at the latest on the 41st move. James D. Allen and Victor Allis showed this independently in 1988.

**How many positions are there in Connect Four?**
On the standard 7×6 board there are 4,531,985,219,092 legal positions.

**Can I play against a friend?**
Yes — choose **A friend** and take turns on the same device. You can type your names, and the score is kept for each board size.

No, but it is tough: it never misses a win or a block it can see and looks many moves ahead. Set up two threats at once, or a threat it can’t reach in time, to beat it.

Yes. **Undo** takes back your last move (and the computer’s reply). Use **Hint** to see the column the computer would pick for you.

Once the page has loaded, yes — the game and the computer run entirely in this tab, and nothing is sent anywhere.

## Reversi

URL: https://justtools.info/games/reversi/

Play Reversi here — the disc-flipping strategy game — against the computer (Easy, Medium, Hard) or a friend. 6×6, 8×8 or 10×10 boards. without an account.

### At a glance

- Reversi on Toolspire: standard rules on the **8×8** board — Black moves first from the four centre discs — plus **6×6** and **10×10** boards.
- Play the computer on **Easy, Medium or Hard**, or a friend on the same device; possible moves are marked, and pointing at one shows which discs would turn.
- Hard searches ahead for about a second per move, values corners, edges and mobility, and plays the **last 12 moves of an 8×8 game perfectly** with an exact endgame search.
- The computer’s solver was checked on the 4×4 board, where perfect play is known: **White wins 11–3**.
- Small boards are solved: on **6×6, White wins 16–20** with perfect play. For 8×8, a 2023 computer study (a preprint by Hiroki Takizawa) reports that perfect play leads to a draw.
- Hints, undo, the full move list in standard notation (f5 d6 …), sound, full screen and keyboard play. Free, with no account.

### Features

- **Three levels**: Easy to learn the rules, Medium for a fair game, Hard for a real fight — it knows the value of corners.
- **See every move**: Dots mark the squares you can play; point at one to see exactly which discs it turns.
- **Passes handled for you**: When a player has no move the turn passes automatically, and the game ends when neither side can move.
- **Learn from hints**: Hint shows the computer’s choice; near the end it tells you the final margin with perfect play.
- **Two players, one screen**: Play a friend with your own names and a running score for each board size.
- **Notation**: Every game is recorded in standard notation, a1 at the top-left — paste it into any Reversi program to study.

### How to play Reversi

1. **Choose an opponent** — Pick **Computer** and a difficulty, and Black (moves first) or White — or **A friend**.
2. **Outflank** — Place a disc so that one or more straight lines of your opponent’s discs lie between it and another of your discs — across, down or diagonally. Those discs turn to your colour.
3. **Pass if you must** — If you have no square that outflanks anything, your turn passes. If you can move, you must.
4. **Count the discs** — When neither player can move, the one with more discs on the board wins.

### Guide

#### Reversi strategy

- **Corners can never be flipped.** Take them when you can — and avoid the squares next to an empty corner (b2, g2, b7, g7 and the edge squares beside the corners), which tend to give it away.
- **Fewer discs early is often better.** Having many discs in the opening limits your own moves; keep your options (mobility) and squeeze your opponent’s.
- **Edges are strong but not always safe.** A lone edge disc can be outflanked along the edge.
- **Parity in the endgame.** Try to make the last move in each region of empty squares.

#### Reversi or Othello?

Reversi is the original name of the game, from the 1880s. The modern version — with the four centre discs placed in a fixed cross pattern and Black moving first — is sold under the trademark Othello, and those are the rules used here. Toolspire is not connected with the Othello trademark owners.

### FAQ

**Where does Reversi run?**
Reversi runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Who moves first in Reversi?**
Black. The game starts with two black and two white discs crossed in the centre (d5 and e4 black, d4 and e5 white), and Black has four possible first moves: d3, c4, f5 and e6.

**What happens if I can’t move?**
You pass and your opponent moves again. If neither player can move, the game ends and the discs are counted.

**Is Reversi solved?**
The 4×4 and 6×6 boards are: White wins both with perfect play (6×6 ends 16–20). For the standard 8×8 board, a 2023 preprint by Hiroki Takizawa reports a computer proof that perfect play is a draw.

**How strong is the Hard computer?**
It looks several moves ahead with alpha-beta search, values corners, edges and mobility, and plays the last 12 moves on 8×8 perfectly. Strong club players can still beat it in the middle game.

**Can I play against a friend?**
Yes — choose **A friend** and take turns on the same device.

**Is my game saved?**
Your settings and scores are kept in this tab on this device. Nothing is sent to a server.

## Checkers

URL: https://justtools.info/games/checkers/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-20

Play checkers here against the computer or a friend: American/English checkers plus international, Brazilian and Russian draughts. without an account.

### At a glance

- Checkers on Toolspire: four rule sets: **American / English checkers** (8×8), **international draughts** (10×10), **Brazilian draughts** (8×8) and **Russian draughts (shashki)** (8×8).
- Every rule that differs between them is built in: backward captures by men, **flying kings**, the rule to **capture the most pieces** (international and Brazilian), and the Russian rule that a man crowned mid-jump keeps jumping as a king.
- Captures are compulsory and multi-jumps must be finished; jumped pieces leave the board only when the move ends, so no piece can be jumped twice.
- Play the computer on **Easy, Medium or Hard** — Hard thinks for about a second a move and follows every exchange to its end — or a friend on one device.
- English checkers is **solved**: Jonathan Schaeffer’s team showed in 2007 (Science) that perfect play from the start is a draw. The game has 500,995,484,682,338,672,639 possible positions.
- Hints, undo, a move list in standard notation (11-15 or e3-d4), optional square numbers, sound and keyboard play. Free, with no account.

### Features

- **The rules you grew up with**: Pick American checkers, international draughts, Brazilian or Russian rules — the board, first player and capture rules follow automatically.
- **Captures made clear**: When a jump is compulsory the tool says so and rings the pieces that must jump; landing squares are marked for the piece you pick.
- **Multi-jumps your way**: Click each landing square in turn, or go straight to the final square when only one route ends there.
- **A computer that fights back**: Three levels, from random-ish moves for beginners to a search that sees exchanges coming.
- **Learn the notation**: Moves are written the standard way for each variant, with optional square numbers on the board.
- **Two players, one screen**: Play a friend with your own names; the board turns so the first player sits at the bottom.

### How to play checkers

1. **Choose the rules** — American / English checkers is the default; pick international, Brazilian or Russian draughts if that is what you play.
2. **Choose an opponent** — Play the **Computer** at Easy, Medium or Hard (and choose your colour), or **A friend** on the same device.
3. **Move diagonally** — Click one of your pieces, then a highlighted square. Men move forward one square on the dark squares; kings move both ways.
4. **Capture by jumping** — Jump over an opponent’s piece to an empty square beyond it. If you can capture, you must — and keep jumping while you can.
5. **Crown and win** — A man reaching the far row becomes a king. You win when your opponent has no pieces left or no legal move.

### Guide

#### How the rule sets differ

|  | American / English | International | Brazilian | Russian |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Board | 8×8 | 10×10 | 8×8 | 8×8 |
| Pieces each | 12 | 20 | 12 | 12 |
| Moves first | Dark | Light | Light | Light |
| Men capture backwards | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Kings | One square | Flying (any distance) | Flying | Flying |
| Must take the most pieces | No | Yes | Yes | No |
| Man reaching the far row mid-jump | Is crowned; move ends | Not crowned unless it ends there | Not crowned unless it ends there | Is crowned and keeps jumping |

#### Checkers strategy

- **Control the centre.** Pieces in the middle of the board have more moves and support each other.
- **Keep your back row.** Leaving your own back-row pieces at home stops the opponent from crowning cheaply.
- **Use the compulsory capture.** Offer a piece so that the forced jump lands your opponent where you can take two back.
- **Trade when ahead.** With a piece more, swapping pieces off makes your advantage count.
- **Kings win endgames.** Get a king early in the endgame — in the flying-king variants one king can control whole diagonals.

#### When the game is a draw

In every variant a game is drawn when the same position, with the same player to move, comes up a third time. Each rule set also ends games that make no progress after a set number of moves by each side, and the tool applies these automatically, warning you in the last ten moves. A player who cannot move loses, whether their pieces are all gone or just blocked.

| Rules | Automatic draw after |
| --- | --- |
| American / English | 40 moves each without a capture or a man moving. Official rules have no automatic limit: a player who refuses a draw offer must show a win within 40 moves. With no draw offers here, the limit applies to every game. |
| International (FMJD) | 25 moves each with only kings moving and no captures; 16 moves each with three pieces (at least one a king) against a lone king; 5 moves each with two pieces or one, including a king, against a lone king. |
| Brazilian | 20 moves each with only kings moving and no captures, which also covers three kings against one. |
| Russian | 15 moves each with only kings moving and no captures, or with three or more kings against a lone king; with kings on both sides and no capture or crowning, 5 moves in 2–3 piece endings, 30 in 4–5 and 60 in 6–7; 5 moves with three pieces against a lone king on the main road (a1–h8). |

### FAQ

**Where does Checkers run?**
Checkers runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Is capturing compulsory in checkers?**
Yes, in all four rule sets: if you can jump, you must, and a multi-jump must be finished. In American checkers and Russian draughts you may choose which capture to make; in international and Brazilian draughts you must take the greatest number of pieces.

**Who moves first in checkers?**
In American / English checkers the dark pieces (often red or black) move first. In international, Brazilian and Russian draughts, light (white) moves first.

**Can kings move more than one square?**
In American checkers, no — a king moves one square diagonally in any direction. In international, Brazilian and Russian draughts kings “fly”: they move any distance along a diagonal and can capture from afar.

**Is checkers solved?**
Yes. In 2007 Jonathan Schaeffer’s team at the University of Alberta published a proof (in Science) that English checkers is a draw with perfect play from the starting position.

**How do I make a multiple jump?**
Click the piece, then click each landing square in turn — or click the final square directly if only one route ends there. The tool won’t let you stop part-way.

**When is a game of checkers a draw?**
When the same position comes up three times with the same player to move, or when nobody makes progress for a set number of moves: 40 moves each without a capture or a man moving in American checkers, 25 moves of kings only in international draughts, 20 in Brazilian and 15 in Russian draughts. Endgames against a lone king have shorter limits in international and Russian rules.

**Can I play against a friend?**
Yes — choose **A friend** and take turns on the same device. The board shows the player who moves first at the bottom.

## Snake Game

### At a glance

- Snake Game on Toolspire: steer with the **arrow keys or W A S D**, **swipe** on a phone or tablet, or use the on-screen arrows. Turns you press quickly are queued, so sharp corners never get lost.
- **Four speeds** (with an option to speed up as you grow), **three board sizes**, **solid walls or wrap-around edges**, and **Bars** or **Pillars** obstacles.
- Every fifth apple brings a **golden apple** worth up to 50 points — the quicker you reach it, the more it pays. Fill every free square and you win.
- Press **Computer plays** to watch it: it plans the shortest path to each apple that still leaves it a way back to its own tail, and often fills almost the whole board.
- Snake began as **Blockade**, a two-player arcade game from Gremlin Industries in **1976**. **Nokia’s Snake**, written by Taneli Armanto, came on the Nokia 6110 in **1998**; Nokia says 350 million copies exist.
- Pick a smooth **modern** look or a blocky **retro phone** screen. Best scores are kept on your device for every speed and board. Free, with no account.

### Features

- **Controls that feel right**: Quick turns are remembered one step at a time, a turn straight back into your neck is ignored, and the game pauses itself if you switch tabs.

- **Make it harder**: Choose a faster speed, a bigger board, obstacles, or turn off wrap-around so the edges are walls.
- **Golden apples**: A bonus apple appears after every fifth apple and fades away — grab it fast for up to 50 points.
- **Watch and learn**: Let the computer play to see how it keeps an escape route open, then press an arrow key to take over.
- **Retro or modern**: A smooth gliding snake on a grass board, or chunky pixels on a phone-style screen.

### How to play Snake

1. **Start moving** — Press an arrow key, swipe on the board or tap **Play**. The snake keeps moving forward on its own.
2. **Steer to the apple** — Turn up, down, left or right to reach the red apple. Each apple makes the snake one square longer and is worth 10 points.
3. **Grab golden apples** — After every fifth apple a golden one appears for a short time. The faster you reach it, the more points it gives — up to 50.
4. **Don’t crash** — Hitting a wall, an obstacle or your own body ends the game. With **Wrap around** on, the edges take you to the other side instead.
5. **Fill the board** — Keep going until the snake fills every free square — the perfect game.

### Guide

#### Scoring

|  | Points | Snake grows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apple | 10 | One square |
| Golden apple | 10–50, more the sooner you reach it | No |
| Every free square filled | You win | — |

#### Tips for a higher score

- **Hug the edges early.** Running along the walls keeps the middle of the board open for later.
- **Don’t chase every apple directly.** When the snake is long, a short cut can wall you in; take the long way round if it keeps a path back to your tail.
- **Follow your tail when in doubt.** The square your tail is leaving is always safe to move into next.
- **Plan your turns early.** You can press two or three turns ahead and they will be played one square at a time.
- **Start slow, then speed up.** Learn a board size at Slow or Normal before trying Fast or Insane.

#### A short history of Snake

The idea began with **Blockade** (1976), a two-player arcade game from Gremlin Industries in which each player leaves a growing wall behind them and tries to outlast the other. The first known home-computer version, *Worm*, appeared for the TRS-80 in 1978, and single-player games where the snake eats items and grows — such as *Snake Byte* and the arcade game *Nibbler*, both 1982 — followed.

Many PC users first met it as *Nibbles*, a sample program that came with QBasic on MS-DOS from 1991. Then in 1998 Nokia put **Snake**, written by Taneli Armanto, on the Nokia 6110 and 5110 phones. It became one of the best-known mobile games ever: Nokia says 350 million copies exist, and in 2012 New York’s Museum of Modern Art named it among the video games it wanted for its collection.

**What was the first Snake game?**
The genre began with Blockade, a two-player arcade game released by Gremlin Industries in 1976. Nokia’s Snake, which made the game famous on phones, followed in 1998.

## Solitaire

URL: https://justtools.info/games/solitaire/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-21

Play classic Klondike solitaire here: draw 1 or draw 3, Vegas scoring, winnable deals, hints, undo and a daily deal. No download, without an account.

### At a glance

- Solitaire on Toolspire: classic **Klondike** rules: build the seven columns down in alternating colours, and the four foundations up by suit from ace to king. Choose **Draw 1** (easier) or **Draw 3** (the classic challenge).
- **Winnable deals only**: before you see a deal, a built-in solver checks it can be won. Even knowing where every card is, only about **82%** of draw-three deals can be won (Blake and Gent, 2019).
- **Windows scoring** (10 for a card on a foundation, 5 for turning a card, a time bonus of 700,000 ÷ seconds), **Vegas** scoring ($52 for the deck, $5 a card back), or no score at all.
- **Tap a card** to send it where it fits, or drag it. Safe cards go up to the foundations by themselves, and **Finish** plays out the rest once every card is face up.
- Unlimited **undo**, **hints**, a **daily deal**, deals you can **share by number**, and a **Solve it for me** button that plays out a winning line.
- Stats for every mode — win rate, streaks, fastest win and best score — and your game in progress are saved on this device. Free, no account.

### Features

- **Every deal can be won**: The solver tries each deal before you get it, so a loss is never the cards’ fault. Turn it off for random deals.
- **Plays the way you do**: Tap to move, drag and drop, or use the keyboard. Left-handed layout puts the stock on the right.
- **Help when you’re stuck**: Hints point to a useful move, undo has no limit, and the game tells you when no useful moves are left.
- **Windows or Vegas scoring**: The original Windows Solitaire points and time bonus, the Vegas money game with limited passes, or no score.
- **A deal a day**: The daily deal is the same for everyone today — and any game can be shared by its number.
- **The bouncing cards**: Win and the cards cascade off the foundations, just like the Windows classic.

### How to play solitaire

1. **Aim for the foundations** — Move all 52 cards to the four foundations at the top, one suit each, from ace up to king.
2. **Build down in the columns** — In the seven columns, put a card on one rank higher of the opposite colour — a red 6 on a black 7. You can move a whole run of cards together.
3. **Turn up hidden cards** — When you move the face-up cards off a column, the card below turns over. Only a king (or a run starting with one) can fill an empty column.
4. **Draw from the stock** — Tap the stock to turn one or three cards onto the waste. The top waste card can be played. When the stock runs out, tap again to turn the waste over.
5. **Win** — Once every card is face up, press **Finish** and the rest go up by themselves.

### Guide

#### Scoring

Standard scores never drop below zero. In Vegas scoring you get one pass through the stock when drawing one card and three passes when drawing three; your running Vegas total is kept with your stats.

| Move | Standard (Windows) | Vegas |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card from the waste to a column | +5 | — |
| Card to a foundation | +10 | +$5 |
| Turning over a column card | +5 | — |
| Card from a foundation back to a column | −15 | −$5 |
| Turning the waste over (draw 1) | −100 | Not allowed |
| Time | −2 every 10 seconds; win bonus 700,000 ÷ seconds (30 s or more) | — |
| Start | 0 | −$52 |

#### Solitaire tips

- **Turn up hidden cards first.** Moves that reveal a face-down card are almost always the best — especially in the columns with the most hidden cards.
- **Don’t empty a column without a king to fill it.** An empty column only takes a king, so clear one when a king is waiting.
- **Think before playing from the waste.** It’s often better to free cards in the columns first and use the stock later.
- **Keep the colours balanced.** If you build a long red-black run, make sure the other colour of the next card is still reachable.
- **Don’t rush cards up.** A card on a foundation can’t hold the next lower card; keep useful cards in play until they are safe to move up.

#### About Klondike

Klondike is the best-known patience game, so well known in the US and Canada that “solitaire” on its own usually means Klondike; in the UK it is often just called patience. Where its name comes from is unknown — the late-1890s Klondike Gold Rush is a popular guess, but nothing proves it.

Its fame today owes a lot to Microsoft, which included Solitaire with Windows 3.0 in 1990, partly to teach people to use a mouse by dragging cards. Whether a random deal can be won is still an open question in mathematics; with every card known, about 82% of draw-three deals can be won, but nobody has worked out the exact figure for the real game, where most cards are hidden.

### FAQ

**Where does Solitaire run?**
Solitaire runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Is every solitaire game winnable?**
No. Some deals can’t be won however well you play — even knowing where every card is, roughly one draw-three deal in five is impossible. With **Winnable deals only** on, the solver checks each deal before you play it, so every game here can be won.

**What is the difference between draw 1 and draw 3?**
In **Draw 1** you turn one card from the stock at a time, so you can reach every card — it’s easier. In **Draw 3** you turn three at a time and can only play the top one, so many cards stay buried; this is the classic, harder game.

**How does Vegas scoring work?**
You “pay” $52 for the deck and win $5 for each card you move to the foundations, so you need 11 cards to break even. You get one pass through the stock drawing one card, or three passes drawing three. Your running total is kept.

**How is the score calculated?**
Standard scoring follows Windows Solitaire: 10 points for a card to a foundation, 5 for playing from the waste to a column or turning over a card, −15 for moving a card back down, and −100 for turning the waste over when drawing one. Time takes 2 points every 10 seconds, and a win adds 700,000 ÷ your seconds.

**Can I play the same deal again or share it?**
Yes. **Restart** replays the current deal, and **Share this deal** gives a link with the game number, so a friend gets exactly the same cards.

**Does it save my game?**
Yes — your game in progress, settings and stats are saved in this browser. Close the tab and carry on later.

**Is it free?**
Yes, completely free with no download and no account. It works on phones, tablets and computers.

Mahjong Solitaire on Toolspire: Play mahjong solitaire here: the classic 144-tile turtle and three more layouts, every deal winnable, with hints, shuffle.

### At a glance

- Mahjong Solitaire on Toolspire: remove the 144 tiles two at a time by matching **free** pairs — a tile is free when nothing lies on top of it and its left or right side is open. Any two **flowers** match, and so do any two **seasons**.
- Four layouts: the classic **Turtle** (144 tiles on five layers), **Pyramid** (120), **Fortress** (116) and **Quick** (72) for a short game.
- **Every deal can be cleared.** Boards are built by playing the game backwards; with random deals, an analysis of ten million turtles found about 3% can’t be cleared at all.
- **Hints** come from a solver, so they point to a pair on a winning line — and the game tells you when the board can no longer be cleared. **Shuffle** rearranges what’s left and keeps it winnable; **undo** has no limit.
- Tiles carry small Latin numbers and letters (E S W N for the winds), so you don’t need to read Chinese characters. Blocked tiles can be shaded to make free ones stand out.
- The computer game was created by **Brodie Lockard in 1981** on the PLATO system. A **daily game**, shareable game numbers, stats and your saved game are all included — free, no account.

### Features

- **Always winnable**: Each deal is built backwards from an empty board, so there is always a way to clear it.
- **Hints that know the way**: A solver picks a pair that keeps the board winnable, and warns you when it no longer is.
- **Easy to read**: Clear, crisp tiles with small index numbers, and shading on blocked tiles.
- **Four layouts**: From the 144-tile turtle to a 72-tile quick game for a coffee break.
- **Shuffle and undo**: Stuck? Shuffle the tiles that are left, or step back as far as you like.
- **Daily game and stats**: Play the same board as everyone today, share a game by its number, and track your fastest clears.

### How to play mahjong solitaire

1. **Find a free tile** — A tile is free if no tile lies on top of it and it can slide out to the left or right — one side must be open.
2. **Match a pair** — Tap two free tiles that are the same to remove them. Any flower matches any flower, and any season matches any season.
3. **Open up the board** — Prefer pairs that free the most tiles: the top of the stacks and the long rows’ ends.
4. **Use help when stuck** — Press **Hint** for a pair that keeps the game winnable, **Undo** to step back, or **Shuffle** when no pairs are left.
5. **Clear the board** — Remove all the tiles to win.

### Guide

#### The tiles

| Group | Tiles | How many |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dots (circles) | 1 to 9 | 4 of each — 36 |
| Bamboo | 1 to 9 (the 1 is a bird) | 4 of each — 36 |
| Characters | 1 to 9, Chinese numerals above 萬 | 4 of each — 36 |
| Winds | East 東, South 南, West 西, North 北 | 4 of each — 16 |
| Dragons | Red 中, Green 發, White (a blue frame) | 4 of each — 12 |
| Flowers | Plum, orchid, chrysanthemum, bamboo — any two match | 1 of each — 4 |
| Seasons | Spring, summer, autumn, winter — any two match | 1 of each — 4 |

#### Tips

- **Work from the top and the ends.** Tiles on top of stacks and at the ends of long rows hold the most other tiles in place.
- **When three of a kind are free, think first.** Removing the wrong two can leave the fourth stuck under its twin.
- **Clear long rows from both ends** so a single tile doesn’t end up blocking a whole row.
- **Save the flowers and seasons** — they match freely, so they’re handy when you need one more move.
- **All four of a kind free? Take them.** Removing a complete set can never hurt.

#### About mahjong solitaire

Mahjong solitaire uses the tiles of the four-player game mahjong, but it is a matching game for one. Brodie Lockard wrote the first computer version, *Mah-Jongg*, in 1981 on the PLATO system, and Activision’s *Shanghai* (1986) brought it to home computers. The classic starting arrangement is called the turtle.

### FAQ

**Where does Mahjong Solitaire run?**
Mahjong Solitaire runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**How do you play mahjong solitaire?**
Tap two matching tiles that are both free to remove them. A tile is free when nothing is on top of it and its left or right side is open. Clear all the tiles to win.

**Is every game winnable?**
Here, yes — each board is built by playing a game backwards, so it can always be cleared. With truly random deals, about 3% of turtle boards can never be cleared.

**Which tiles match?**
Identical tiles match. The exceptions are the flowers and the seasons: any flower matches any other flower, and any season matches any other season.

**What if there are no moves left?**
Press **Shuffle** to rearrange the remaining tiles in the same places — the new arrangement can still be cleared — or **Undo** to go back.

**What does the hint do?**
It asks a solver for a pair that keeps the board winnable and highlights it. If the board can no longer be cleared, it tells you so you can undo or shuffle.

**Can I play on my phone?**
Yes. The board fits phone screens; for bigger tiles, try the Pyramid or Quick layout or full screen.

### How to play Word Guess

3. **Narrow it down** — Use what you learn: keep green letters where they are, move yellow ones, and avoid grey ones. The keyboard keeps track for you.
4. **Solve within six** — Find the word in six guesses or fewer to win and keep your streak going.
5. **Play again** — Press **Next word** for another, or switch to the **daily word**.

### Guide

#### Repeated letters

A letter is coloured only as many times as it appears in the answer. If you guess GEESE and the answer is THOSE, only the final E turns green — the other two Es are grey, because THOSE has just one E. Exact matches are coloured first, then letters in the wrong spot from left to right.

#### Tips for solving in fewer guesses

- **Start with common letters.** Words with E, A, R, O, T, L, I, S and N give you the most information.
- **Use new letters early.** On your second guess, try mostly letters you haven’t used yet, even if you suspect a word.
- **Remember repeated letters.** Words like LEVEL, GEESE or APPLE trip people up — the answer can repeat a letter.
- **Think about word endings.** -ER, -LY, -ED and -ING patterns (in six letters) narrow things fast.
- **Save hard mode for later.** Normal mode lets you spend a guess on testing letters.

#### Word list credits

Accepted guesses come from the public-domain ENABLE word list. Answers were chosen from the common-word levels of the English Speller Database (SCOWL), which draws on Alan Beale’s public-domain 12dicts lists, and then checked to leave out rude and offensive words.

## Chess

URL: https://justtools.info/games/chess/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-21

Play chess here against the computer at five levels, from beginner to master, or with a friend on one screen. Hints, undo, move list, PGN and FEN.

### At a glance

- Chess on Toolspire: every rule is built in: **castling**, **en passant** and **promotion**, check and **checkmate**, **stalemate**, and draws by **threefold repetition**, the **fifty-move rule** and too little material to mate.
- Play the computer at **five levels** — Beginner, Casual, Club, Strong and Master. It thinks in a background thread with alpha-beta search, so the page never freezes; at Master it looks around ten moves ahead.
- Play **a friend** on one device, take moves back with **undo**, ask for a **hint**, and step back through the game in the move list.
- Legal moves are shown as dots when you pick up a piece; drag pieces or tap the start and end squares. Choose your piece on promotion, or always queen.
- **Copy the game as PGN** or the position as **FEN**, and start from any position you paste in. Your game in progress is saved on this device.
- Claude Shannon wrote the first paper on computer chess in **1950**; in **1997** IBM’s Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov 3½–2½. Free, no download, no account.

### Features

- **A level for everyone**: Beginner looks one move ahead and leaves pieces hanging; Master thinks up to four seconds a move and is hard to beat.
- **Learn as you play**: Legal-move dots, hints from the engine, and undo as often as you like.
- **Two players, one board**: Play a friend on a phone, tablet or computer and flip the board when you need to.
- **Review your game**: Step back and forward through every move with the arrows or the move list.
- **PGN and FEN**: Copy your game to analyse elsewhere, or paste a FEN to practise any position.
- **Never freezes**: The computer thinks in the background, so the board stays smooth even at the strongest level.

### How to play chess here

1. **Choose your opponent** — Play the **Computer** — pick a level and your colour — or **A friend** on the same device.
2. **Make a move** — Drag a piece, or tap it and then tap a highlighted square. White moves first.
3. **Use the help** — Press **Hint** for a suggestion, **Undo** to take a move back, or step through the moves with the arrow keys.
4. **Finish the game** — Checkmate the king to win. Stalemate, repetition, the fifty-move rule and bare kings are draws — or resign when it’s hopeless.
5. **Save it** — Copy the PGN to keep the game or study it in another program.

### Guide

#### How the pieces move

| Piece | Moves | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| King | One square any way; castling with a rook | — |
| Queen | Any distance along ranks, files and diagonals | 9 |
| Rook | Any distance along ranks and files | 5 |
| Bishop | Any distance along diagonals | 3 |
| Knight | An L: two squares one way, one square to the side; jumps over pieces | 3 |
| Pawn | One square forward (two from its first square); captures diagonally; promotes on the last rank | 1 |

#### Special rules

- **Castling**: the king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps to the other side. Not allowed if either has moved, if a square between them is occupied, or if the king is in check, passes through check or ends in check.
- **En passant**: when a pawn moves two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved one square — but only on the very next move.
- **Promotion**: a pawn reaching the far rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight.
- **Draws**: stalemate (no legal move but not in check), the same position three times, fifty moves each without a capture or pawn move, or not enough material left to checkmate.

#### Credits

The chess pieces are the Chessnut set, copyright 2015 Alexis Luengas, used under the Apache License 2.0 (a copy is served with the piece images). The computer player was written for this site.

**Can I play chess against the computer at no cost?**
Yes — choose **Computer**, pick a level from Beginner to Master, and play as White, Black or a random colour. There’s no account and nothing to download.

**How strong is the computer?**
Beginner looks one move ahead with deliberate mistakes, Casual sees simple tactics, Club plays solid chess, Strong thinks about a second and a half a move, and Master thinks up to four seconds and looks around ten moves ahead.

**Can two people play on one device?**
Yes — choose **A friend** and take turns. Use **Flip** to turn the board.

**How do I castle or promote a pawn?**
To castle, move the king two squares toward the rook; the rook follows automatically. When a pawn reaches the last rank you choose its new piece (or switch on “Always promote to a queen”).

**What is PGN and FEN?**
PGN records a whole game move by move; FEN describes a single position. Copy either to use in other chess software, or paste a FEN under “Set up a position” to play from it.

**Is my game saved?**
Yes, your game in progress, settings and results are saved in this browser.

Play Spider Solitaire here with 1, 2 or 4 suits: build king-to-ace runs to clear the table. Undo, hints, Windows scoring and stats. No download.

### At a glance

- Spider Solitaire on Toolspire: two packs, **104 cards**: 54 dealt into ten columns (six cards in the first four, five in the rest), and 50 in the stock, dealt **ten at a time** — one on each column — when no column is empty.
- Put any card on one a rank higher, but only a **run of one suit** moves as a group. A complete run from **king to ace** in one suit leaves the table by itself; clear all eight to win.
- Choose **1 suit** (all spades — most games can be won), **2 suits** (spades and hearts) or **4 suits**, the classic, where good players win about **one game in three**.
- **Windows scoring**: start at 500, lose a point for every move (and every undo), and gain 100 for each completed suit.
- **Tap a card** to move it and the cards on it, or drag; **hints** point to the most useful move; **undo** has no limit. Long columns squeeze to fit the screen.
- Spider came to Windows in **Microsoft Plus! 98**. Stats by difficulty, shareable deals and your game in progress are kept on this device — free, no account.

### Features

- **One, two or four suits**: Start with all spades, step up to two suits, and take on the classic four-suit game when you’re ready.
- **Smart tap to move**: Tap a card and it goes to the best place — onto its own suit if it can.
- **Hints that skip the pointless**: Hints prefer building in suit and turning cards up, and never suggest shuffling a run back and forth.
- **Undo all the way**: Step back as far as you like (each undo costs a point, as in Windows).
- **Fits any screen**: Ten columns on a phone, with long columns squeezed to stay in view.
- **Stats and streaks**: Win rate, best score, fastest win and streaks, kept separately for each difficulty.

### How to play Spider Solitaire

1. **Build down** — Move a face-up card onto any card one rank higher — a 6 on any 7. Kings can only go into an empty column.
2. **Keep runs in one suit** — A run of one suit (say 9-8-7 of hearts) can be moved together; mixed-suit runs can only be moved a card at a time.
3. **Turn up hidden cards** — When you move the face-up cards off a column, the card below turns over. Empty columns accept any card or run.
4. **Deal when stuck** — Tap the stock to deal one card onto every column. You can’t deal while a column is empty.
5. **Clear the suits** — A full run from king to ace in one suit is removed automatically. Remove all eight to win.

### Guide

#### Difficulty levels

| Suits | Cards | What changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 suit | 8 × spades | Every card can join any run — the gentle way to learn. |
| 2 suits | 4 × spades, 4 × hearts | Runs of two suits block each other; planning matters. |
| 4 suits | 2 × each suit | The classic and toughest game: roughly one in three is won with good play. |

#### Spider Solitaire tips

- **Turn up face-down cards** as early as you can — especially in the columns with the most of them.
- **Build in suit whenever you can.** A same-suit run can move as one; a mixed run is stuck.
- **Empty a column** and keep it for a while: it is the most powerful space on the table.
- **Put cards on kings and high cards** before low ones, so runs have room to grow.
- **Before dealing, tidy up** — a new row covers every column, so fix what you can first.

#### About Spider

Spider is a two-pack patience in which the ten columns are built down by rank and cleared one complete suit at a time. Microsoft added Spider Solitaire to Windows in the Microsoft Plus! 98 pack with one-, two- and four-suit versions; an earlier Windows 3.x version was written in 1991 by John A. Junod. Hoyle’s Rules of Games puts the chance of winning the classic game with good play at about one in three.

### FAQ

**Where does Spider Solitaire run?**
Spider Solitaire runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**How do you play Spider Solitaire?**
Build the ten columns down in rank — any card on one a rank higher — and move runs of one suit together. When a column holds a full king-to-ace run of one suit, it is removed. Clear all eight runs to win; deal from the stock when you run out of moves.

**Which is easiest: 1, 2 or 4 suits?**
One suit is by far the easiest, because every run is in suit and can move as a group. Two suits is a good middle step, and four suits is the classic, hardest game.

**Why can’t I deal new cards?**
The rules don’t allow dealing while any column is empty. Move a card or run into the empty column first.

**How is the score worked out?**
As in Windows: you start with 500 points, lose 1 for every move or undo, and gain 100 for each suit you complete.

**Can every game be won?**
No. Most one-suit games can be won, but in the four-suit game only about one in three is won even with good play.

**Does it save my game?**
Yes — your game in progress, settings and stats are saved in this browser.

## FreeCell

URL: https://justtools.info/games/freecell/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-21

Play FreeCell solitaire here with the same numbered deals as Microsoft FreeCell (1 to 1,000,000). Hints, undo, a solver and stats. without an account.

### At a glance

- FreeCell on Toolspire: all **52 cards are dealt face up** into eight columns (four of seven, four of six). Four **free cells** each hold one card; the **foundations** build up by suit from the ace.
- Columns build down in **alternating colours**. Runs move together through the free cells and empty columns: up to **(free cells + 1) × 2 to the power of empty columns** cards at once.
- Deals use **Microsoft FreeCell’s numbering**, 1 to 1,000,000 — type a number to play the same game as on Windows. Game **#11982** is the only one of the original 32,000 that can’t be won.
- Almost every deal can be won: one 2018 study found just one impossible deal in about **84,000**. A built-in solver gives **hints** and can **solve the game for you**.
- **Tap a card** to send it to its foundation, a column or a free cell, or drag runs. Safe cards go up by themselves; **undo** has no limit.
- Paul Alfille created FreeCell on the PLATO system in **1978**. Stats, streaks, shareable deals and your game in progress are saved on this device — free, no account.

### Features

- **Microsoft-numbered deals**: Game #1 here is game #1 on Windows — play famous deals or share any game by its number.
- **Smart moves**: Tap a card and it goes to the best place; runs move in one go, as many as the free cells allow.
- **A solver that helps**: Hints come from a real search, and it tells you when a position can no longer be won.
- **Undo without limits**: Step back as far as you like and try another line.
- **Left- or right-handed**: Put the foundations on the side you prefer.
- **Streaks and stats**: Win rate, fastest win and your best streak, saved in this tab.

### How to play FreeCell

1. **Free the aces** — Move cards off the aces and twos so they can go up to the foundations, built by suit from ace to king.
2. **Build down in alternating colours** — Put a card on one a rank higher of the other colour — a black 7 on a red 8.
3. **Use the free cells** — Park any single card in one of the four free cells. Use them sparingly: each empty cell lets you move longer runs.
4. **Empty a column** — An empty column takes any card or run and doubles how many cards you can move together.
5. **Finish** — Win by moving all 52 cards to the foundations. Safe cards go up by themselves.

### Guide

#### How many cards can I move at once?

A “supermove” is a shortcut for moving the cards one at a time through the free cells and empty columns — the game does it for you, so you only drag the whole run.

| Free cells | Empty columns | Run you can move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 0 | 5 cards |
| 3 | 0 | 4 cards |
| 2 | 1 | 6 cards (3 into the empty column) |
| 4 | 1 | 10 cards (5 into the empty column) |
| 0 | 0 | 1 card |

#### FreeCell tips

- **Look before you move.** Every card is visible, so plan where the low cards will go.
- **Keep free cells empty** as long as you can — each one adds a card to the runs you can move.
- **Aim for an empty column**; it is worth more than a free cell.
- **Dig out aces and twos first**, especially those deep in a column.
- **Don’t fill the last free cell** unless it wins you something right away.

#### About FreeCell

FreeCell grew out of Baker’s Game, which Martin Gardner described in Scientific American in 1968; Paul Alfille changed it to build in alternating colours and wrote the first computer version on the PLATO system in 1978. Microsoft’s version numbered its deals, and of the original 32,000 only game #11982 has no solution. Across billions of deals, about one in 84,000 can’t be won.

### FAQ

**Where does FreeCell run?**
FreeCell runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Is every FreeCell game winnable?**
Almost. Of Microsoft’s original 32,000 deals only #11982 can’t be won, and a 2018 study of 8.6 billion deals found about one impossible deal in 84,000.

**Are these the same games as Microsoft FreeCell?**
Yes — the deals use the same numbering, so typing a game number gives the same layout as the Windows game.

**Why can’t I move a long run?**
You can only move as many cards as the free cells and empty columns allow: (free cells + 1) × 2 for each empty column. Free up a cell or a column and try again.

**What do the free cells do?**
Each of the four cells holds one card, to get it out of the way. They’re the key to FreeCell — and the fewer you use, the more freedom you keep.

**Can the computer solve it for me?**
Yes. **Solve it for me** plays out a winning line from where you are (that game won’t count in your stats), and **Hint** shows the next move of a winning line.

**Is it free?**
Yes, free with no download and no account. Your game and stats are saved in this tab.

## Ludo

URL: https://justtools.info/games/ludo/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-21

Play Ludo here for 2 to 4 players: against the computer or with friends on one device. Star safe squares, captures, extra rolls on a six. without an account.

### At a glance

- Ludo on Toolspire: play **2, 3 or 4 players**: you against the computer (Easy or Smart), or friends taking turns on one phone, tablet or computer.
- Roll a **six** to bring a token out of your yard; a six also gives you **another roll** — but **three sixes in a row** lose the turn.
- Land on an opponent to **send them back to their yard** (and roll again). Start squares and **star squares are safe**; your home column is yours alone.
- Race once round the board, up your coloured home column and into the centre — you need the **exact roll** to get home. First with all four tokens home wins.
- Tokens step square by square, the die tumbles, and tokens you can move glow. Optional rules let you switch off the capture bonus or the three-sixes rule.
- Ludo comes from **Pachisi**, played in India for centuries, and was sold under the name Ludo — Latin for “I play” — in England from **1896**. Free, no account.

### Features

- **You against the computer**: Play one, two or three computer opponents. Smart captures, runs for safety and gets tokens home.
- **Pass and play**: Two to four friends take turns on one device — perfect for the family.
- **Star safe squares**: Start squares and the star on every arm are safe, as on Indian Ludo boards.
- **Clear moves**: Movable tokens glow, single moves can play themselves, and every roll and capture is announced.
- **Your house rules**: Turn the extra roll for a capture or the three-sixes rule on or off.
- **Pick up later**: The game in progress is saved on your device after every move.

### How to play Ludo

1. **Roll to start** — Tap the die. You need a **six** to move a token out of your yard onto your coloured start square.
2. **Move a token** — Tap a glowing token to move it forward by the number rolled, clockwise round the board.
3. **Capture and stay safe** — Landing on an opponent sends them home to their yard. Tokens on start and star squares can’t be captured.
4. **Go up your home column** — After a full lap, turn into your coloured column. Only your tokens can go there; you need the exact roll to reach the centre.
5. **Win** — Get all four tokens home first. A six, a capture and getting home each earn another roll.

### Guide

#### Ludo rules at a glance

| Situation | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Leaving the yard | Needs a six; the token goes to your start square |
| Rolling a six | Move, then roll again |
| Three sixes in a row | Turn lost (can be switched off) |
| Landing on an opponent | They go back to their yard; you roll again (can be switched off) |
| Safe squares | The four start squares and the four star squares |
| Finishing | Exact roll needed to reach home; getting a token home earns another roll |

#### Ludo tips

- **Get tokens out early** — having two or three on the board gives you choices with every roll.
- **Park on safe squares** when an opponent is within six squares behind you.
- **Capture when you can** — it costs your opponent a whole lap and gives you another roll.
- **Don’t race one token alone**; spread your moves so a single capture can’t ruin your game.
- **Watch the squares in front of opponents’ start squares** — tokens there are easy targets for newly released pieces.

#### About Ludo

Ludo is a simplified form of Pachisi, the cross-and-circle race game of India. It was sold in England as Ludo from 1896 — the name is Latin for “I play” — and is still one of the most-played board games in India, where it is often played with star safe squares.

**Where does Ludo run?**
Ludo runs in this tab on Toolspire. What you type or drop in is not sent to us and is not stored on a server.

**Can I play Ludo with the computer?**
Yes — choose **Computer** and play Red against one, two or three computer players, at Easy or Smart.

**Can I play Ludo with friends?**
Yes, on one device: choose **Friends (pass & play)** and two to four players take turns.

**Do you need a six to start in Ludo?**
Yes. A token can only leave the yard on a six, and a six also gives you another roll.

**What are the safe squares?**
The four coloured start squares and the four star squares. A token on them can’t be captured.

**What happens if you roll three sixes?**
By default you lose the turn, as in the standard rules. You can switch this rule off.

**Is my game saved?**
Yes — the game in progress and your record against the computer are saved in this browser.

#### Hangman tips

- **Start with vowels** — E, A, O and I appear in most words.

- **Look at the length and the gaps.** A word ending in _ _ _ might be -ING or -ION.
- **Use the category.** In Countries, think of endings like -IA and -LAND.
- **Save the whole-word guess** until you’re fairly sure — a wrong one costs a life.

#### About Hangman

Hangman is a guessing game for two or more players, usually played with pencil and paper: one player thinks of a word and draws a blank for each letter, and the others guess letters until they solve it or the drawing is finished. Its origins are unclear, but Alice Gomme’s Traditional Games of England, Scotland, and Ireland (1894) describes a version called “Birds, Beasts and Fishes”.

## Snakes and Ladders

URL: https://justtools.info/games/snakes-and-ladders/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Snakes and Ladders on Toolspire: Play Snakes and Ladders here: against the computer or with friends on one device. Four boards, house rules for 100 and sixes.

### At a glance

- Snakes and Ladders on Toolspire: play **2, 3 or 4 players** — you against the computer, or friends taking turns on one phone, tablet or computer.
- Land on the foot of a **ladder** to climb it; land on a **snake’s head** and slide down to its tail. First to **square 100** wins.
- Choose a board: **Classic**, **Easy climb** for younger players, the longer **Snake pit**, or a **Random** board that is new every game.
- Set your house rules: **bounce back**, **stay put** or **still win** when you roll past 100, **another roll on a six**, and **a six to start**.
- Each board shows **how many rolls a game takes on average**, worked out exactly from the board and your rules.
- The game comes from ancient India, where it was called **Moksha Patam**; ladders stood for virtues and snakes for vices. Free, no account.

### Features

- **You against the computer**: Play Red against one, two or three computer players who roll by themselves.
- **Pass and play**: Two to four friends share one device and take turns.
- **Four boards**: Classic, Easy climb, Snake pit, or a fresh random board every game.
- **Your house rules**: Bounce back off 100, need the exact roll, or win with any roll; extra roll on a six; a six to start.
- **Animated moves**: Tokens step square by square, climb ladders and slither down snakes, with sounds you can switch off.
- **Pick up later**: The game in progress is saved on your device.

### How to play Snakes and Ladders

1. **Roll the die** — Tap the die or press Space. Your token moves forward that many squares, starting from off the board.
2. **Climb ladders** — If you finish on the foot of a ladder, climb straight up to its top.
3. **Watch out for snakes** — If you finish on a snake’s head, slide down to its tail.
4. **Roll a six** — A six gives you another roll (you can turn this rule off).
5. **Reach 100** — The first player to reach square 100 wins. Choose what happens if you roll past it.

### Guide

#### The boards

| Board | Ladders | Snakes | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Classic | 7 | 8 | Everyday games — more snakes than ladders, as on old Indian boards |
| Easy climb | 10 | 5 | Young children and quick games |
| Snake pit | 6 | 10 | A long, nail-biting race |
| Random | 8 | 9 | Something new every game |

#### House rules for square 100

- **Bounce back** (the default): roll too high and you count up to 100 and back again — on 97, a 5 takes you to 98.
- **Stay put**: you need the exact number; if the roll is too high, you don’t move.
- **Still wins**: any roll that reaches 100 wins, which makes games shorter.
- A study in The Mathematical Gazette (1993) worked out game lengths this way, treating the board as a Markov chain — the same maths shows the average on each board here.

#### About Snakes and Ladders

Snakes and Ladders began in India as part of a family of dice board games that also includes Pachisi, the ancestor of Ludo. Known as Moksha Patam, it was a lesson in morals: ladders were virtues such as generosity and humility, snakes were vices such as anger and theft, and reaching the top meant liberation (moksha). The Jain version is called Gyan Chaupar.

The game reached England in the 1890s — the earliest known English version was registered in 1892 — and later the United States, where it is sold as Chutes and Ladders. In Hindi it is called Saanp Seedhi, in Telugu Vaikunthapali and in Tamil Parama Padam. The phrase “back to square one” is thought to come from it.

**Can I play with friends?**
Yes, on one device: choose **Friends (pass & play)** and two to four players take turns.

**What happens if you roll more than you need to reach 100?**
You choose: bounce back off 100 (the default), stay where you are, or win anyway.

**Do you need a six to start?**
Not by default — everyone starts off the board and moves straight away. Switch on **Need a six to start** for that house rule.

**How long does a game take?**
Each board shows the average number of rolls one player needs, worked out from the board and your rules — around 38 on the Classic board with bounce-back.

#### About word search

Word search puzzles — also called word find or word seek — hide a list of words in a grid of letters. The first published word search is credited to Norman E. Gibat, who printed one in the Selenby Digest in Norman, Oklahoma, on 1 March 1968; teachers there soon asked for copies for their classes, and the puzzle spread from there.
